pages.description: S.2 provides about $70 billion through 2029 for immigration enforcement and border security. It increases the number of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers; expands resources for detention and deportation operations; invests in border security technology; and supports other federal immigration enforcement activities.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 adds funding for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) staff, surveillance, aircraft, and boats. The money is “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1] and remains available until “September 30, 2029” [1]. Section 201 funds staff and operations “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1] Section 101 funds Border Patrol staff for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1] Section 103 funds “Upgrades and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] and “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]

points.title: Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of wildlife water.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of wildlife water.

  • Because Interior reported that deploying border staff and equipment reduced damaging traffic: “By deploying personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service identified crossing-related litter: “Perhaps one of the most well known of the impacts of illegal immigration is the litter left behind” [3].
  • Because That litter spoiled wildlife water: “Water sources near this contamination are often so fouled by pollution that wildlife can no longer use them.” [3]
  • So Section 201's staffing and section 103's surveillance funds support patrols of the kind Interior credits with these local reductions. Where added patrols cut crossings through wild areas, they can reduce this pollution. Protecting wildlife water serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
points.con_html:
Response The cited local gains do not establish that S.2's added patrols would reduce, rather than shift, the traffic that pollutes wildlife water.

  • Because Interior reported local reductions: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3]
  • So Enforcement can move traffic into remote wild areas as well as reduce it. Reductions “in a number of areas” do not show that S.2's added patrols would lower the litter reaching wildlife water overall. The PRO needs evidence that the added patrols would reduce such traffic near wild water sources rather than redirect it.

points.title: Better interception protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Better interception protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.

  • Because Section 103 limits funding for southwest and northern border towers to systems tested and accepted by CBP “to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1]
  • Because CBP reported faster interception with autonomous towers: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that “unauthorized trails and roads have been created on the Forest by illegal foot and vehicle traffic.” [3] Their spread “damages and destroys cactus and other sensitive vegetation; disrupts or prohibits revegetation; disturbs wildlife, their security and travel routes; causes soil compaction and erosion” [3].
  • Because Crossing-related damage left a fence protecting endangered habitat “ineffective in restricting livestock use” [3]. The result was habitat loss: “This fence damage has allowed the destruction of endangered species habitat to continue” [3].
  • So Funding staff and faster detection strengthens the ability to stop damaging traffic and fence damage. That protects plants, wildlife habitat, and soil from destruction, which [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response A shorter detection-to-capture time does not establish less damage to trails, plants, or fences.

  • Because The tower report describes a narrower result: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3]
  • So Response speed is not total travel through habitat or avoided fence damage, and enforcement can move traffic into wild areas. The PRO has not connected faster interception to less damaging traffic overall.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Surveillance baseline: CRS says P.L. 119-21 provides $6.17 billion for inspection and surveillance technology. Sources: [5].

points.title: Intercepting unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful introduced species.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Intercepting unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful introduced species.

  • Because In March 2025, Interior described harm from unlawful border activity: “national parks, wildlife refuges and the species they protect are adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6].
  • Because Border operations have reduced the activity carrying these risks: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Added staffing and surveillance support interception of this traffic. Less unlawful travel through parks and refuges can reduce one route by which harmful species spread there. Reducing such introductions is a way to protect nature.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats immigration interception as invasive-species control without showing which introductions it would reduce.

  • Because Interior lists lands and species as “adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6], but does not identify the species or how they arrive.
  • Because Seeds can travel on people. The National Park Service explains: “Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing.” [7]
  • So The missing step is keeping species from reaching habitat. Catching people after entry does not itself show that seeds have been kept out. Neither the list of harms nor the general report of reduced border activity shows that S.2 would reduce these introductions, or by which pathway.

points.title: Preventing damaging crossings also addresses a source of destructive wildfires.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Preventing damaging crossings also addresses a source of destructive wildfires.

  • Because The Forest Service documented the link: “Large numbers of warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators have caused wildfires that have destroyed valuable natural and cultural resources.” [3]
  • Because S.2 supports an established way to reduce the underlying activity. Interior reported that border operations “have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Supporting interception before people travel and camp through natural areas strengthens prevention of these ignitions. Avoiding fires that destroy nature gives [NAME] another reason to favor S.2.
points.con_html:
Response The sources do not connect S.2's added interceptions to fewer abandoned campfires in the forests at issue.

  • Because The Forest Service identifies “warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators” [3] as a cause of wildfires.
  • Because The same testimony reports that enforcement beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3]
  • Because Section 201 funds CBP staff and operations “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • So The PRO relies on Interior's general report of reductions in some areas. The fire evidence comes from a forest where enforcement pushed traffic into the backcountry, so added patrols do not necessarily mean fewer people camping there. The PRO needs evidence that S.2's patrols would reduce crossings in fire-prone wildlands rather than shift them.

points.title: Funding Border Patrol's other duties supports early fire warnings and calls for firefighting help.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Funding Border Patrol's other duties supports early fire warnings and calls for firefighting help.

  • Because Section 101 pays to “hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1]
  • Because Those agents provide fire warnings. After agents spotted smoke near the border in April 2025, “They promptly contacted fire crews from the Forest Service and Mexico.” [8]
  • Because U.S. crews put out the resulting spot fires: “U.S. fire services swiftly put out spot fires caused by embers that blew across the border, while Mexican crews battled the main blaze to the south.” [8]
  • Because Agents also summoned help during a 2021 Jacumba Wilderness fire: “El Centro Station notified the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) of the situation.” [9] The resulting response succeeded: “The combined resources and firefighting efforts were able to control the fires.” [9]
  • So S.2 supports staff who detect fires and bring in the crews needed to control them. This strengthens protection of natural areas from spreading fire.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

points.title: Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.

  • Because The Forest Service reported that border enforcement took officers away from conservation: “The law enforcement efforts in response to cross-border violators and smugglers of controlled substances diverts our officers from other management and resource protection activities.” [3]
  • Because Interior documented “intelligence-supported joint patrols on Interior and USFS managed lands.” [2] It reported a division of duties: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2]
  • Because Alongside section 201's immigration staffing, section 103 funds “Enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals, at the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1]
  • So S.2 supports the border-enforcement side of this division of work. Preserving land officers' time for protecting natural resources serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
points.con_html:
Response A division of duties within a joint patrol does not show that S.2's funding protects land officers' time for conservation.

  • Because Interior describes patrols that used officers from both agencies: “Border Patrol agents frequently conduct joint patrols with Interior law enforcement personnel on Interior-managed lands, including national parks, wildlife refuges, and public lands.” [2]
  • Because Its account of one operation says: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2]
  • So This shows assigned roles within joint operations that themselves draw on land officers. The Forest Service's 2006 complaint about diversion does not show that S.2's added CBP funding would reduce the enforcement work those officers now do. The PRO has not shown that the bill would free their time for conservation.

points.title: Patrol support helps land managers carry out planned burns that care for vegetation.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Patrol support helps land managers carry out planned burns that care for vegetation.

  • Because The Forest Service uses fire for land care as well as fighting unwanted fires: “The Forest Service works to both fight wildland fires and to use prescribed fires as a tool to manage vegetative resources.” [3] Prescribed fires are planned burns.
  • Because Security is part of doing that work: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” [3] The same testimony states: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.” [3]
  • So Section 101's support for duties outside immigration and customs enforcement backs staff who help secure these work areas. Enabling people to carry out this care for vegetation supports the active defense of nature that [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The testimony does not distinguish help with fire suppression from help with planned burns.

  • Because The testimony describes clearing fire areas and guarding firefighters: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” [3] It adds: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.” [3]
  • Because The discussion covers both kinds of fire work: “during prescribed fires or fire suppression operations” [3]. Prescribed fires are planned burns.
  • So Unspecified security help at fires does not establish that Border Patrol support enabled planned burns. Without that step, the claimed support for vegetation care rests on an assumption about which fire work agents helped with.

points.title: Better aircraft and boats support protection of marine life against illegal fishing.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Better aircraft and boats support protection of marine life against illegal fishing.

  • Because Section 103 funds upgrades and new equipment for air and marine response, as quoted above.
  • Because CBP air and marine crews joined a 2024 operation that “located and stopped a total of 19 Mexican fishermen engaged in illegal fishing” [10].
  • Because The Coast Guard described the purpose as “safeguarding our valuable resources and protecting the delicate marine environment” [10].
  • So S.2 funds equipment used in this work. Strengthening the ability to stop illegal fishing protects marine life and serves [NAME]'s concern for nature.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The April 2026 law also covered “air and marine support; and the purchase or lease of various vehicles, vessels, aircraft, and unmanned aerial systems.” The 2024 fishing result came from a joint Coast Guard, CBP and Texas operation. Sources: [5], [10].

points.title: Better aircraft can add to the capacity CBP has occasionally lent to oil-spill cleanup.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Better aircraft can add to the capacity CBP has occasionally lent to oil-spill cleanup.

  • Because Section 103 funds upgrades and new equipment for rapid air response, as quoted above.
  • Because During the 2010 Gulf spill, CBP reported that its crews were “providing airspace de-confliction and flight advisories to the numerous government agencies that are participating in the clean up and containment efforts.” [11] This means helping cleanup aircraft share the airspace safely.
  • So S.2's platform funds add to the fleet whose crews have been called on for this support. The use is occasional and depends on which aircraft are bought, but it can add to the capacity to coordinate pollution cleanup. Helping contain oil pollution serves [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 2010 spill report describes the P-3 as a specialized surveillance and command aircraft. The reviewed record does not identify a §103 plan buying that capability. Sources: [11], [1].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 adds funding for border operations and immigration enforcement. Section 202 alone gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “$31,075,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1], “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1].

points.title: It pays for flights that pollute the air and heat the planet.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It pays for flights that pollute the air and heat the planet.

  • Because Section 202 funds deportation transport: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Such transport includes flights: “ICE’s air transportation is being carried out through a network of chartered flights” [12].
  • Because These flights emit heat-trapping pollution: “US immigration enforcement flights are producing hundreds of thousands of metric tonnes of climate-damaging carbon emissions” [12].
  • Because They also pollute the air around airports: “planes frequently idling, taking off and landing in the same communities contributes to local air pollution” [12].
  • So Added transport funding supports flights with both kinds of pollution. [NAME]’s wish to protect the environment from pollution gives a reason to oppose that support.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: §202's $31.075 billion is a shared pool with no flight line. CRS reports a plan to use FY2025 reconciliation funds to offset $350 million in Transportation and Removal Operations in FY2027. The targeted search did not find a flight-program funding record separating added flights. Sources: [13], [1].

points.title: It funds detention operations that keep wildlife away from facility sites.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It funds detention operations that keep wildlife away from facility sites.

  • Because Section 202 pays to keep enforcement facilities in use: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1] It also funds “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]
  • Because Dilley, Texas, is part of ICE’s detention network, and its operation depends on ICE funding. The site had been idled in 2024 “when funding for the contract with ICE was terminated and the facility was idled” [14]. In March 2025 its operator announced that “it has agreed under an amended intergovernmental services agreement (IGSA) between the City of Dilley, Texas, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to resume operations” [14].
  • Because ICE’s assessment found that the cleared site offered “limited natural habitat for native wildlife” but expected wildlife to avoid it during use: “migratory birds and other wildlife will likely avoid the proposed project area during construction activities and during operations.” [15]
  • So S.2 gives ICE more resources to run facilities with this effect. The disturbance at this already-cleared site is small, but protecting wildlife still gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added support.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Dilley's assessment compares operation with never building. Operations resumed in March 2025 under an agreement running to March 2030. The targeted search did not find a record tying S.2 to Dilley's scale or duration. Sources: [15], [14], [13].

points.title: It supports air pollution from detention facilities and their vehicles.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It supports air pollution from detention facilities and their vehicles.

  • Because Section 202 funds “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” [1] and “Funding for fleet maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because ICE’s Dilley assessment identifies operating sources of air pollution: “vehicular use and emergency generators during the operation phase.” [15]
  • So Added money for these facilities and vehicle fleets supports activities that emit air pollution. [NAME]’s wish to prevent pollution gives a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Dilley assessment says extended generator use would occur during power disruptions, and its comparison assumes no facility. Sources: [15].

points.title: It supports detention operations that risk polluting land and water.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It supports detention operations that risk polluting land and water.

  • Because Section 202 funds the running of enforcement facilities through “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” [1].
  • Because Social Circle’s city government warns that operating ICE’s planned detention center would “risk sewage overflows into nearby land and water” [16].
  • Because Maryland’s assessment of the Williamsport warehouse proposal explains the same operating risk. Its agencies estimate sewage flow at “more than seven times the existing projected flow for the facility’s prior commercial use.” [17]
  • Because They explain the risk: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17].
  • Because The waterways at issue support wildlife: “A number of State-listed Endangered species, Species in Need of Conservation, and other Rare species rely on the waters in the vicinity of the Warehouse property.” [17]
  • So More operating money supports a detention network pursuing warehouse conversions with documented sewage risks, as Social Circle’s plans show. Protecting land, water, and the wildlife that depends on them gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that support.
points.con_html:
Response The sewage argument leaves out barriers to the conversions that existed before June 9, 2026.

  • Because Social Circle's city manager described a condition on water access: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity.” [18]
  • Because The April 15 preliminary court order barred Williamsport's detention conversion: “Defendants are enjoined during the pendency of this lawsuit from construction and renovation at the warehouse located at 16220 Wright Road, Williamsport, Maryland 21795 (the “Williamsport Warehouse”) for the purposes of operating the warehouse as a detention and processing facility;” [19]
  • Because Maryland's warning concerns exceeding existing sewer capacity: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17].
  • Because Its required response is to address that capacity: “Any necessary upgrades must comply with applicable State permitting requirements and be funded by DHS.” [17]
  • So S.2's operating money does not itself lift the water restriction, the court order, or the permit requirements. The warnings do not show that the bill makes operation beyond sewer limits more likely. That requires a link from the added funds to the unsafe operation despite those barriers.

points.title: It equips border patrols whose off-road driving damages desert wilderness.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It equips border patrols whose off-road driving damages desert wilderness.

  • Because Section 201 funds “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1] for immigration enforcement.
  • Because At Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, an interagency agreement allows emergency off-road patrols: “This agreement authorizes border enforcement agents to drive off-road in wilderness under exigent or emergency circumstances that involve threats to human health and safety.” [20]
  • Because In 2012, the National Park Service reported that, since the agreement took effect, “monitoring data have shown that off-road-vehicle impacts have increased” [20].
  • Because Its account of undesignated roads and trails explains the physical harm: “These incursions damage soils, vegetation, and wildlife habitat.” [21]
  • So Extra money for these patrols supports off-road driving that damages soil, plants, and habitat. Protecting wild places gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html:
Response More border-patrol staffing does not by itself mean more damaging off-road driving at Organ Pipe.

  • Because Section 201 funds several uses of personnel: “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1].
  • Because The agreement behind the PRO's example allows agents to patrol “on foot or on horseback” [22].
  • Because The Park Service later documented staffing growth aimed at reducing vehicle use: “The U.S. Border Patrol Ajo Station has increased its Horse Patrol Unit (HPU) with the recent graduation of agents through the class. The Ajo Station HPU patrols at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in an effort to reduce mechanized equipment in the wilderness.” [23]
  • So Personnel funding and damaging vehicle use are separate steps. The PRO's 2012 damage trend does not show that S.2 increases such driving or keeps it going when it would otherwise stop. The same site's horse patrols show why staffing growth alone cannot establish that link.

points.title: It puts forest protection and restoration crews at risk of removal.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It puts forest protection and restoration crews at risk of removal.

  • Because Sections 201 and 202 pay immigration enforcement personnel “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Those activities reach forest workers. In 2025 Border Patrol arrested a firefighter whose work included “clearing fallen trees and other debris to prevent the Bear Gulch fire, a 9,000-acre blaze, from growing” [24]. He was later “quietly deported to Mexico” [24].
  • Because ICE has also removed tree-planting crews. After a 2007 raid on a contractor replanting burned land in Boise National Forest, “Ten of the workers were deported to Mexico and four others were released pending an immigration hearing” [25].
  • Because That work had a short planting window. The Forest Service spokesman explained: “You have to plant in cooler times, when the ground is moist” [25].
  • Because Delayed replanting threatens nature. In 2025 the Forest Resources Association warned that without timely reforestation, “these lands risk erosion, habitat loss” [26].
  • So More capacity to arrest and remove these workers puts time-sensitive forest care at risk. Protecting forests gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added capacity.
points.con_html:
Response The forestry examples do not show that S.2 raises the risk of leaving needed forest work without crews.

  • Because Follow-up reporting on the 2025 incident found continued crew assignments: “Both of the private crews have active agreements with the Forest Service and have been assigned to new fires.” [27]
  • Because The 2007 report describes an effort to replace arrested workers: “For now, Olson said his office is working with the company to get replacement workers as soon as possible.” [25]
  • Because The forestry association argues for more temporary work visas. Its proposed remedies include: “An exemption for forestry workers from the H-2B visa cap to address the reforestation backlog.” [26]
  • So Arrests alone do not establish the risk of forest work lacking crews; continued assignments and replacement efforts also matter. A warning about harm from delayed planting does not show that S.2 raises the chance of those delays. The PRO has not connected the added enforcement funds to a greater risk of unfilled planting or forest-protection work.

points.title: It strengthens surveillance tools that can deter people from defending nature.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It strengthens surveillance tools that can deter people from defending nature.

  • Because Section 103 funds CBP aircraft and related equipment: “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]
  • Because That branch uses surveillance drones to help other law enforcement. A 2025 CBP statement reported that “MQ-9 Predators are supporting our federal law enforcement partners in the Greater Los Angeles area, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with aerial support of their operations.” [28]
  • Because CBP has used such tools at environmental protests: “Customs and Border Protection responded to the protests with its MQ-9 Reaper drone” [29]. The Standing Rock movement sought “to protect water, the climate, and Indigenous sovereignty” [29]. During a 2020 pipeline dispute, “CBP flew drones over its planned pipeline route and over the homes of anti-pipeline activists” [28].
  • Because Researcher Nathan Goodman identifies the barrier to participation: “Surveilling protesters is a concerning use of drones, as it may chill or repress speech, association and assembly protected by the First Amendment.” [28]
  • So S.2's platform money can enlarge or upgrade the aerial fleet whose drones have been lent for monitoring environmental defenders, although the bill does not specify drones. The added risk of deterring their participation gives [NAME], who values taking part in defending nature, a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: §103 states a 'rapid air and marine response' purpose and names no drones. No platform list or protest-mission frequency series was found. Sources: [1].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 adds money for border security, criminal investigations and immigration enforcement: “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]; “to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1]. Section 102 funds Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) staff and operations for “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1].

points.title: It helps find and rescue children suffering sexual abuse.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps find and rescue children suffering sexual abuse.

  • Because Section 102 sets aside money for more investigators and analysts: “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” [1].
  • Because Their funded task is “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1]. The money also funds training for investigators and local police: “to train such personnel and State and local law enforcement regarding identifying victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1].
  • Because Representative Lee described the unmet need: “Today, more than 89,000 children depicted in child sex abuse material remain unidentified.” [2]. In fiscal year 2024, an international operation hosted by HSI's victim-identification lab led to the “identification and assistance of over 140 victims.” [3].
  • So More investigators, analysts and trained police strengthen the work of finding these children and helping them escape abuse. Protecting children who cannot secure their own safety serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and their chance of a safe childhood.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

points.title: It supports teaching children and families how to prevent online sexual abuse.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It supports teaching children and families how to prevent online sexual abuse.

  • Because Section 102 adds money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1] and for HSI's operations.
  • Because HSI's Project iGuardian teaches children, parents and community groups through “in-person presentations” [3]. Its wider campaign aims to “prevent and combat online child sexual exploitation and abuse” [3].
  • So S.2's general HSI funds can help sustain or expand this teaching, although the bill does not direct money to it. The teaching gives families tools to spot danger and seek help before abuse takes hold. Helping children protect themselves serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect general staffing funds for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to more education for children and families.

  • Because Project iGuardian uses “special agents and subject matter experts” [3] to give presentations. More presentations therefore require their time, not just a larger agency budget.
  • Because November 2025 reporting described agents being reassigned to immigration work, “dramatically slowing investigations into child exploitation and sex trafficking” [4]. Agents' time was therefore under competing demands.
  • Because Section 102 funds agents and support staff for “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. Its specific child-protection training requirement concerns “such personnel and State and local law enforcement” [1], not presentations to families.
  • So The PRO identifies a teaching program that depends on agents' time, and training investigators to identify victims does not add that time. This leaves the step from general funds to more teaching uncertain. It does not show that general funds could not reach this work.

points.title: It strengthens protection and help for people forced into sex or labor.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens protection and help for people forced into sex or labor.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents and “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because This work includes criminal investigations of coercion: “Homeland Security Investigations initiated 1,686 criminal investigations related to sex trafficking and forced labor, leading to 2,545 arrests.” [5]. These are fiscal year 2024 results.
  • Because An HSI-backed sex-trafficking case involving adults and children brought an abuser to justice: “the defendant was found guilty at a jury trial and sentenced to 380 months” [3] after using “violence, false imprisonment and the use of drugs.” [3].
  • Because HSI's victim program also ensures survivors “are informed of their rights” [3] and “receive necessary assistance” [3]. Earlier added funds enabled that program “to create 76 new full-time positions” [3].
  • So More resources for investigations and victim support strengthen both escape from coercion and help afterward. Freedom from forced sex and work, access to help, and justice against abusers serve [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and equal opportunities.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s examples do not show that S.2 would add trafficking investigations or survivor-support staff under the changed assignment policy.

  • Because November 2025 reporting described agents being reassigned to immigration work, “dramatically slowing investigations into child exploitation and sex trafficking” [4]. This directly challenges an unchanged link between HSI’s budget and its trafficking work.
  • Because The earlier expansion of the Victim Assistance Program came from targeted funding: “From FY 2020 to FY 2023, the VAP received congressional enhancement funds” [3]. That precedent shows what targeted money did, not what general HSI funding would do.
  • Because Its money must support “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]. That limits how these dollars may be spent; it does not say which other work they reach.
  • So The PRO has not shown that this funding would reach trafficking cases under those assignments, or add the survivor-support jobs its precedent describes. This weakens the step from HSI's budget to this work. It does not show that general funds could not help.

points.title: It strengthens the response to scams against older people and other victims.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It strengthens the response to scams against older people and other victims.

  • Because Section 102's staffing and operating funds support HSI's criminal work, including “wire fraud, identity theft, bank fraud” [3].
  • Because Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported that in fiscal year 2024, “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases” [3], producing “121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” [3]. HSI also investigated romance scams: “HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” [3] cases that year.
  • So More capacity to investigate these scams, secure convictions and seize criminals' proceeds strengthens protection against financial exploitation. [NAME] has a reason to protect victims' resources and seek justice for them, including strangers targeted because of age or trust.
points.con_html:
Response The fraud totals do not establish more protection against scams from S.2 under HSI’s changed priorities.

  • Because The fraud results are explicitly past results: “In FY 2024, HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” [3] cases and “258 elder fraud cases” [3]. They describe an earlier distribution of investigators’ work.
  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” [6]. Section 102 provides broad “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1], without reserving funds for elder or romance fraud.
  • So The PRO needs a reason to expect added investigators’ time to reach these scams under the priorities in place at the vote. The 2024 totals do not provide it.

points.title: It supports justice for victims of atrocities abroad.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It supports justice for victims of atrocities abroad.

  • Because Section 102 adds resources for HSI staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because HSI's human rights center helps prosecute people for “human rights violations and war crimes” [3] committed before they entered the United States. In fiscal year 2024, it “supported more than 180 investigations” [3] related to suspected war criminals.
  • So Resources for investigating and prosecuting these crimes strengthen efforts to hold abusers accountable. [NAME]'s concern for justice extends to victims abroad, including people [NAME] has never met.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The center's 180-plus investigations cover a mixed mission including removal and other agencies, and §102 excludes HSI's immigration-enforcement mission, so the count may include work §102 cannot fund. Sources: [3], [1].

points.title: It adds resources to intercept drugs that cause overdoses.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It adds resources to intercept drugs that cause overdoses.

  • Because Section 103 adds $3.45 billion for inspection equipment, air and marine response, surveillance and related work: “$3,450,000,000 for the following” [1]. Its purposes include “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders” [1].
  • Because The funded work includes “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1], meaning ingredients used to make drugs. ICE describes the resulting danger as “the synthetic drugs that fuel overdose deaths” [3].
  • So Finding and intercepting these drugs keeps seized supplies from reaching people. More resources for that work strengthen protection for people at risk of overdose, whose lives matter to [NAME].
points.con_html:
Response Cheap replacement weakens the inference from a seized shipment to lower overall drug exposure.

  • Because Drug-policy researchers Jonathan Caulkins and Peter Reuter explain: “But traffickers can easily replace what is seized.” [7] Their stated mechanism is that fentanyl is cheap to make and easy to move: “It is absurdly cheap for high-level traffickers to replace seizures.” [7]
  • Because A 2026 systematic review (search through April 2025) treated some seizures as enforcement disruptions. The results it describes point in different directions: local or regional studies linked seizures to more overdoses nearby or the next year, while a Florida county study linked fewer seizures to more deaths. These are associations, not estimates for S.2's border resources. [8]
  • So The replacement mechanism challenges the PRO's step from seized shipments to lower net exposure and overdose risk. It does not deny that seized drugs themselves stay off the street, and neither the review nor cheap replacement proves that added interception has no benefit.

points.title: It strengthens the capacity to take convicted violent offenders into immigration custody.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It strengthens the capacity to take convicted violent offenders into immigration custody.

  • Because Section 202 funds staff “to carry out immigration enforcement activities” [1] and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1].
  • Because This work includes taking custody of people convicted of attacks on children. ICE reported a January 2026 arrest of a man convicted of “first-degree rape of a child” [9]: “upon his release from prison Jan. 2, ICE took him into custody for removal to Mexico.” [9].
  • So Added staff and transport resources support taking convicted violent offenders into custody after prison release. Custody limits their access to potential victims in the community, giving [NAME] a reason to support protection against further attacks.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The cited man was already in ICE custody in January 2026. §202(9) reserves at least $350 million for specified non-cooperating jurisdictions and covers more than violent convictions. The reviewed record does not identify the offense shares of arrests added by S.2. Sources: [9], [10], [1].

points.title: It strengthens criminal investigations of terrorist threats.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It strengthens criminal investigations of terrorist threats.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents, support staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because HSI's National Security Unit “supports counterterrorism investigations within HSI.” [3]. HSI's fiscal year 2024 results in this work included “70 criminal indictments” [3], and ICE credited HSI with helping produce “terrorism-related disruptions.” [3].
  • So Resources for investigating and disrupting terrorist threats strengthen protection for people exposed to violence. [NAME]'s concern includes potential victims who are strangers.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s earlier counterterrorism results do not show that new funds would restore or expand investigators’ work on threats.

  • Because The report places the “70 criminal indictments” [3] in fiscal year 2024. In January 2026, senators cited reporting that “a major joint FBI-HSI investigation into illicit Iranian oil shipments” [6] had “suffered from the redeployment” [6] of investigators.
  • Because Section 102 provides “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1] for eligible HSI work. It does not assign investigators back to these cases or reserve a counterterrorism staff increase.
  • So The PRO’s missing link is investigators’ time on threats under the assignment policy in place at the vote. An earlier criminal-case total does not show that added agency funds would supply it.

points.title: It supports protection of essential services from cyberattacks.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It supports protection of essential services from cyberattacks.

  • Because Section 102 adds resources for HSI staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. HSI's criminal work includes protecting computer systems.
  • Because HSI's Operation Cyber Centurion fights attacks on “major utilities, healthcare, public education” [3], financial systems and emergency services. In fiscal year 2024, it “disrupted 195” [3] computer break-ins and attacks.
  • So Resources to stop attacks on hospitals, utilities and emergency services protect people who depend on those services for safety and care. This serves [NAME]'s concern for people least able to protect themselves during an emergency.
points.con_html:
Response The cyberattack count does not establish more protection for essential services from S.2.

  • Because The report says, “In FY 2024, OCC disrupted 195” [3] intrusions and attacks. That measures the existing operation’s work, not the effect of additional funding under the later assignment policy.
  • Because The January 2026 letter reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” [6]. Section 102 funds broad “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1], without a separate allocation of cyber investigators or operating funds.
  • So The PRO cannot carry the earlier work pattern forward without showing how the new money would reach cyber investigations. The count supplies no such link to additional protection for hospitals or utilities.

points.title: It supports rescues of migrants in life-threatening danger.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 It supports rescues of migrants in life-threatening danger.

  • Because Section 103 funds “new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities” [1]. Section 101 funds Border Patrol personnel for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1].
  • Because These teams perform rescues. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) reported that an April 2024 aircrew located lost migrants, landed, and treated an unresponsive man who was “severely dehydrated and suffering from heat exhaustion.” [11]. A Border Patrol emergency medical technician then took over his care.
  • Because CBP explained the mechanism: “The ability of our agents to rapidly transition from a law enforcement role to conduct rescue operations where they can deliver immediate medical aid is crucial to saving lives.” [11].
  • So More resources for air response and rescue personnel strengthen lifesaving help for people stranded at the border. [NAME] has a reason to protect them regardless of immigration status.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

points.title: It adds resources for recordings that support fair review of officers' conduct.
points.pro_html:
Point 11 It adds resources for recordings that support fair review of officers' conduct.

  • Because Section 202(3) includes “body-worn cameras” [1] among the uses of its added technology funds.
  • Because ICE's February 2025 camera policy makes wider use depend on “appropriated funding resources.” [12]. It directs officers to record “interactions with the public during Enforcement Activities” [12] in areas where the camera program operates.
  • Because The policy allows review of recordings “to assess, evaluate, or address any officer action” [12], including “civil liberties, or any other issues.” [12].
  • So Added resources for camera use support evidence about how officers treat people. Evidence for reviewing disputed encounters serves [NAME]'s concern that people facing government power be treated justly.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: P.L. 119-86 separately provided $20 million for camera procurement, deployment and operations. AP (July 10, search extracts only) reported DHS's statement that more than half of ICE field offices had cameras with the rest due within 60 days, and a member of Congress's account that fewer than a third of officers had them with all due by end of July. No crosswalk separates the $20 million from §202(3), and coverage is unverified (Q10, Q15). Sources: [1], [12], [13], [14].

points.title: It makes more resources available for medical care in immigration custody.
points.pro_html:
Point 12 It makes more resources available for medical care in immigration custody.

  • Because Section 202 funds ICE personnel across its directorates and “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1].
  • Because ICE's fiscal year 2026 budget identifies medical care as part of those operations: “Custody Operations program’s detainee healthcare activities” [15]. These services include “medical, mental, and dental health services” [3].
  • So More resources available to staff and run custody health services support care for people who depend on the government for treatment. Protecting people in this dependent position serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people regardless of nationality.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2021 OIG review found remote locations, competing opportunities, difficulty offering competitive pay and cumbersome hiring limit medical staffing, and that vacancy rates are hard to measure. Healthcare is an existing activity with no assigned increase. Sources: [16], [15].

points.title: It provides resources to protect agency workers from injury.
points.pro_html:
Point 13 It provides resources to protect agency workers from injury.

  • Because The bill funds staff training and equipment, including money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel” [1] and corresponding HSI and immigration-enforcement funds.
  • Because A DHS inspector general report describes protective gear as “equipment to protect them while on duty.” [17]. It also identifies defensive training “to mitigate and prevent assaults” [17].
  • So Resources for protective equipment and safety training support safer work. Providing protection against known job hazards is part of treating workers justly, which gives [NAME] a reason to favor this funding too.
points.con_html:
Response The safety report identifies failures in training delivery, not a funding shortage that S.2 is shown to repair.

  • Because The 2018 report already described standard protective gear: “officers receive a ballistic vest and outer carrier” [17]. It also found unclear training requirements: “ICE does not clearly define requirements for refresher training” [17].
  • Because The report traced uneven training to discretion over its timing and content. It recommended that ICE “Mandate that law enforcement officers complete refresher” [17] training quarterly. S.2 funds agencies to “hire, pay, train, and equip” [1] staff but does not set that schedule or repair the guidance.
  • So The value of gear and training does not show that S.2 would improve workers’ protection. The PRO has not connected the appropriation to better equipment or delivery of the training its source identifies as missing.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 would add money for immigration arrests, detention and deportation through September 2029. Section 202 gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) another “$31,075,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1], including “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]. Section 201 also funds Customs and Border Protection (CBP) staff “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]. The Brennan Center explains the connection to existing practices: “The money will allow the department to continue the Trump administration’s mass deportation strategy” [18]. Human Rights Watch describes the package as proceeding “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [19].

points.title: It finances more confinement of people who pose no public safety threat and favors custody over release under monitoring.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It finances more confinement of people who pose no public safety threat and favors custody over release under monitoring.

  • Because The strategy being funded already includes “locking up immigrants who pose no public safety threat” [18].
  • Because Section 202(9) sets aside an arrest and custody fund of “Not less than $350,000,000” [1].
  • Because For this pool, the bill rules out spending on release or alternatives such as check-ins, except when existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” [1].
  • So The bill adds capacity to take people's freedom under an enforcement strategy that reaches people who pose no safety threat. It also excludes less restrictive uses of the targeted pool. Just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose financing that loss of freedom.
points.con_html:
Response The absence of a public safety threat does not establish that the funded custody is needless or unjust.

  • Because Custody has a purpose beyond preventing violence. The Supreme Court tests detention against a period “reasonably necessary to secure removal” [20] and the purpose of “assuring the alien’s presence at the moment of removal” [20].
  • Because Section 202(9)'s release restriction governs “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” [1] and exempts releases “required by existing law” [1]. It neither bars all spending on monitored release nor removes a right to release.
  • So Preventing flight before a timely removal can justify custody without a finding of dangerousness. The PRO does not show that monitoring would serve that purpose in the cases it objects to. Its move from no safety threat to unjust confinement leaves out that question.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It pays to extend enforcement with a record of singling people out by race or background.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It pays to extend enforcement with a record of singling people out by race or background.

  • Because Section 202 funds more federal personnel and local participation through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. These agreements “allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” [23].
  • Because Human Rights Watch found federal agents in Los Angeles “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [19].
  • So More staff and a wider enforcement network extend the reach of an operation with documented race-based stops. Exposure to detention because of someone's background conflicts with equal opportunities and just treatment.
points.con_html:
Response The Los Angeles findings do not establish that the added staff and local agreements would spread race-based stops under the approach reported before the vote.

  • Because Human Rights Watch locates those findings in the “campaign of raids and detentions throughout the summer of 2025 in Los Angeles” [19].
  • Because On May 5, CBS reported Homan's account that “Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [24]
  • Because The same report says ICE had prioritized “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” [24].
  • So Evidence about the earlier operation does not establish that the funded expansion would carry race-based stopping forward under the reported change in tactics. The CBS report is an official's account and does not address the local agreements the PRO also relies on. This does not show that such stops have ended.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It expands the government's ability to seek removal in a system that obstructs some detained people's access to legal help.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It expands the government's ability to seek removal in a system that obstructs some detained people's access to legal help.

  • Because Section 202 funds government attorneys “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” [1]
  • Because An inspection of Camp East Montana found violations including “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.” [25]
  • So A person unable to reach a lawyer has less chance to challenge the government's case. Increasing removal capacity in a system with these barriers increases exposure to removal without a fair chance to defend oneself. Concern for just treatment extends to these strangers.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that adding government lawyers puts more people through hearings while they cannot reach counsel.

  • Because Section 202(7) pays attorneys “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” [1]
  • Because The inspection cited at Camp East Montana found “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.” [25] This is evidence about access to communications at that facility.
  • So The missing link is added exposure to hearings with blocked legal help. The inspection does not establish which additional proceedings these hires enable or that people in those proceedings face that barrier.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It sustains detention with documented dangers to children's and sick people's health.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It sustains detention with documented dangers to children's and sick people's health.

  • Because Section 202 pays for “facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Human Rights Watch documented conditions in Florida in 2025 including “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” [19].
  • Because Before the vote, Senator Kim described a seriously ill man he met in detention: “He should have been in a hospital, but, instead, he was isolated in that cramped room for 5 months.” [26]
  • Because Children also face unsafe conditions: “In Dilley, families described receiving food with worms and mold, tainted water, and inadequate education.” [25]
  • Because The new operating money lasts through September 2029, although these are “federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.” [27]
  • So The bill sustains a system with these hazards and adds money it can use without new yearly approval. That makes withholding a future year's operating funds a weaker tool for demanding safer conditions.
  • So Financing continued detention without the needed reforms exposes people dependent on their jailers to further harm. Protecting children and sick people gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion for detention capacity and $29.85 billion for other functions, available FY2025–FY2029. The targeted search did not find a with-and-without-S.2 detention estimate. Sources: [21].

Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It funds separation of children from the parents whose care they need.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It funds separation of children from the parents whose care they need.

  • Because Parental detention has already harmed citizen children: “U.S. citizen children have experienced family separation as a result of a parent being detained.” [25]
  • Because The harm includes loss of care during a medical crisis. A father “was detained on his way to the hospital in Texas to deliver milk to his premature 12-day-old daughter.” [25]
  • So Paying for more arrests, detention and removals increases exposure to the loss of daily parental care, including for infants who need it urgently. Protecting dependent children gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Senate Budget minority staff put ICE's unobligated 2025-law money at $62 billion at the end of May 2026. The targeted search did not find a with-and-without-S.2 arrest estimate, including one specific to parents. Sources: [22], [25].

Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It spreads harm through communities beyond the people arrested.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It spreads harm through communities beyond the people arrested.

  • Because Senator Smith described help needed during Minnesota's enforcement operation: “Churches and neighbors organized mutual aid and delivered prescriptions to folks who couldn't leave their own homes.” [28] She also described “food deliveries for people who were afraid to go to the grocery store.” [28]
  • Because Children suffered continuing trauma and missed school: “Kids traumatized by these tactics and still not back in school.” [28]
  • Because Educational harm reaches children of U.S.-born parents too. A research review reports that “negative academic impacts following immigration enforcement actions extended to U.S.-born students with U.S.-born parents.” [29]
  • Because The same review describes lasting effects, with “one study finding notable reductions in 4-year college enrollment following a large-scale worksite raid in Texas in 2018.” [29]
  • So Funding more such operations extends a threat to access to food and medicine, children's well-being and their schooling. Protecting vulnerable people and equal chances in life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these wider harms to communities.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO carries the effects of particular past operations into its forecast without accounting for the change in approach before the vote.

  • Because CBS reported that Homan had been charged with “winding down the Minneapolis operation” [24] and described ICE's shift toward “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” [24].
  • Because The PRO's education examples concern past enforcement actions, including a “large-scale worksite raid in Texas in 2018.” [29]
  • So Those examples do not establish how S.2 changes exposure to the operations behind the food, medicine and school disruptions. The PRO supplies no link from the added funding under the revised approach to those wider harms.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It funds enforcement under a paused but unrescinded home-entry policy without requiring judicial warrants.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It funds enforcement under a paused but unrescinded home-entry policy without requiring judicial warrants.

  • Because Representative Thompson reported that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) used earlier funding to “break into homes without warrants” [2].
  • Because The final bill adds enforcement money without the proposed judicial-warrant requirement: “It does not require officers to get judicial warrants.” [2]
  • Because In May, the DHS secretary wrote that ICE “has not rescinded the memorandum; however, I have paused the practice of entering an illegal alien’s residence who is subject to a final order of removal with an I-205” [30], “while I assess the policy.” [30]
  • So S.2's operating money would fund operations under which such entries could resume after the review, and it adds no condition requiring a judge's approval. Protecting people from unchecked entry into their homes is part of treating strangers justly, so that risk gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the funding.
points.con_html:
Response The absence of a new warrant condition does not establish that S.2 revives a home-entry practice paused before the vote.

  • Because On May 8, the DHS secretary wrote: “I have paused the practice of entering an illegal alien’s residence who is subject to a final order of removal with an I-205” [30]. An I-205 is ICE's removal warrant.
  • Because The secretary described the pause as lasting “while I assess the policy.” [30] This was an announced pause during review.
  • So The June 9 comparison includes that pause. Omitting a new funding condition does not itself restart the practice or establish added exposure to it.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: S.2 is compared with a law in force that already financed expansion, including $29.85 billion for staff, 287(g) and other functions and $62 billion unobligated at the end of May 2026. Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It funds operations with a record of violence and punishment of peaceful advocates.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It funds operations with a record of violence and punishment of peaceful advocates.

  • Because Human Rights Watch documented agents “using excessive force against peaceful protestors, legal observers, volunteer street medics, and journalists outside an ICE detention facility.” [19]
  • Because The stakes include death. The Brennan Center describes the funding dispute as following “the killing of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.” [18]
  • Because Representative McCollum reported: “Peaceful demonstrators were threatened and detained for exercising their First Amendment rights.” [31]
  • So More funding without the needed reforms extends the risk of injury, death and unjust detention to people caught in enforcement operations and those peacefully helping or defending others. Protecting them and treating peaceful advocacy justly gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO predicts more violent encounters from the earlier record without assessing the change in command and tactics before the vote.

  • Because By May, CBS reported that the commander who led the wider sweeps had been removed: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [24]
  • Because The same report describes ICE's move toward “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” [24].
  • So These changes bear directly on how agents encounter people during operations. The PRO does not explain why added funding under this approach would increase the violent encounters or punishment of peaceful advocates in its examples.

Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: It strengthens indiscriminate monitoring of immigrants and citizens.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It strengthens indiscriminate monitoring of immigrants and citizens.

  • Because Section 103 funds “Upgrades and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] Section 202 also funds “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations” [1].
  • Because The Brennan Center explains the wider effect: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [18]
  • So This adds capacity to collect people's information without distinguishing those involved in wrongdoing from everyone else. Just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose exposing strangers to that intrusion and scrutiny.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO equates more surveillance capacity with indiscriminate collection without establishing what makes the funded collection indiscriminate.

  • Because Section 103 funds surveillance “along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] Section 202 funds “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations, including improvements to fee collections and body-worn cameras.” [1]
  • Because The Brennan Center predicts capabilities that “facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [18] Its account does not trace these spending lines to a collection practice without a fair purpose or limit.
  • So The quoted provisions establish funded purposes, not unfair selection or use of people's information. The PRO has not supplied the link from these appropriations to the indiscriminate intrusion on which its justice argument rests.

Size unresolved; a balance does not by itself show no increment. Sources: [21], [22].

points.title: Removing workers and their spending power threatens other families' jobs and earnings.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 Removing workers and their spending power threatens other families' jobs and earnings.

  • Because Immigrant workers support other workers' jobs: “significant job losses among immigrant workers could mean less demand for other work done by U.S.-born workers.” [29]
  • Because Such losses have already reached a local industry. Minnesota's enforcement operations harmed its restaurant industry, contributing to “about 4,600 lost jobs and $71 million in lost wages in the first three months of 2026” [29].
  • So Funding further removals threatens jobs and earnings beyond those of the people removed. Lost pay makes basic needs harder to meet for families with little money. Protecting their livelihoods and chances in life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the added removal funding.
points.con_html:
Response The Minnesota job losses do not measure the effect of S.2's added removal funding.

  • Because The restaurant example concerns Minnesota operations “between December 2025 and April 2026” [29]. CBS later reported that Homan had been charged with “winding down the Minneapolis operation” [24].
  • Because The source's general mechanism is conditional: “significant job losses among immigrant workers could mean less demand for other work done by U.S.-born workers.” [29]
  • So The figure reflects that operation, so it says little about how much added removal funding would cost other families. This weakens the PRO's local example. It does not answer the general link from lost immigrant jobs to lower demand for other work.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.2 adds funding for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol staff and operations through September 30, 2029: “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]. Section 102 provides “$7,450,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel and to provide other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) must use this money for “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions” [1].

points.title: Supports cases against people who persecute others for their identity or beliefs.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Supports cases against people who persecute others for their identity or beliefs.

  • Because Section 202 funds ICE staff across its branches, including investigators and lawyers, “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because ICE's human rights center handles immigration cases involving “individuals who have persecuted others based on race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion” [2].
  • Because HSI also investigates crimes including “torture, genocide, recruitment and use of child soldiers” [2].
  • Because HSI's work includes “Supporting efforts to return violators to their home countries to face justice for the crimes they committed there.” [3]
  • Because Past funding helped ICE's human rights center “increase staffing and, in turn, to generate more case leads.” [2]
  • So Section 102 adds resources for criminal human rights investigations; section 202 adds resources for immigration cases against persecutors.
  • So Persecution attacks the differences [NAME] values accepting. Holding persecutors to account gives [NAME] a reason to fund this work.
points.con_html:
No point-specific CON is provided.

Shared objection Changed staff assignments undermine the PRO's reliance on old HSI mission descriptions to predict how new resources would be used.

  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” [4].
  • Because Section 102 requires its funds to serve “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions” [1].
  • So This limit excludes a use of section 102's money. It does not restore former assignments or identify support for the particular investigations, interview services, and victim assistance the PRO selects. Old descriptions of agency work cannot establish how the added resources would reach those activities.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The earlier human-rights money was earmarked (“not less than $5,300,000”), so it is a weaker precedent for general funds. Sources: [2].

points.title: Supports protection for people threatened for expressing different political views.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Supports protection for people threatened for expressing different political views.

  • Because HSI already investigates foreign governments' efforts to silence people abroad: “HSI already works to investigate allegations of transnational repression” [5].
  • Because These threats include “incidents targeting individuals critical of foreign authoritarian regimes, like the Iranian regime and the Communist Chinese Party” [5].
  • So Section 102 adds resources for investigators whose existing work includes countering these threats. Protecting critics from coercion defends their ability to hold and express views others reject. [NAME]'s acceptance of people despite disagreement gives a reason to support that protection.

  • Because HSI provides “interpreters and translation services, allowing victims to fully understand and communicate their needs as they navigate legal, medical and support systems.” [7]
  • Because Its victim support uses a “culturally sensitive approach” [6]; interview specialists “create neutral, safe spaces where victims are empowered to share information in their own words.” [6]
  • So Section 102 supports staff and services that help people explain experiences across differences in language and culture. Funding that work directly serves [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand people who are different.

points.title: Supports practical help for victims in HSI cases regardless of immigration status.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Supports practical help for victims in HSI cases regardless of immigration status.

  • Because HSI's victim specialists “support and provide services to victims, regardless of their immigration status” [8].
  • Because Their work includes more than interviews: “HSI's special agents and Victim Assistance Program Specialists (VAPs) focus on removing victims from dangerous situations and ensuring their basic needs are met.” [7]
  • Because HSI describes this support as “delivery of services in a nonjudgmental manner.” [8]
  • So Section 102 supports help for victims in HSI cases across differences in immigration status. Treating these people as worthy of care puts acceptance into practice, including when someone disagrees with their entry or stay. [NAME]'s tolerance gives a reason to fund that help.
