points.title: Supports rescue that puts people's safety ahead of nationality or immigration status.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Supports rescue that puts people's safety ahead of nationality or immigration status.

  • Because Section 101 provides money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1]
  • Because Customs and Border Protection (CBP) documents Border Patrol rescues of people who were “lost, in distress, or abandoned by smugglers.” [9]
  • Because CBP explains its rescue priority: “When someone is in distress, their safety and well-being come before their citizenship, nationality, or immigration status. The same resources used for border security are immediately directed to those in need.” [9]
  • So Section 101 adds resources for personnel whose work includes these rescues. Helping people across nationality and immigration status treats them as people worth protecting. That gives [NAME] a reason to support the funding.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

points.title: Makes more money available for records that let officials check complaints of biased treatment.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Makes more money available for records that let officials check complaints of biased treatment.

  • Because Section 202 includes funding for “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations, including improvements to fee collections and body-worn cameras.” [1]
  • Because ICE's 2025 camera policy ties wider use to funding: “Enterprise-wide implementation shall be dependent on availability of appropriated funding resources.” [10]
  • Because The policy describes cameras as “accurately documenting events, actions, conditions, and statements made by encountered individuals” [10].
  • Because Senior ICE officials may use recordings to examine officers' actions and rights concerns: “permitted to review BWC recordings to assess, evaluate, or address any officer action, technological, policy, legal, operational, financial, civil liberties, or any other issues.” [10]
  • So This funding supports a record of encounters that officials can use to assess complaints of mistreatment, including bias against different groups. Making people's treatment and accounts available for review serves [NAME]'s commitment to listening to and accepting people across those groups.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.2 adds almost $70 billion for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS): “providing almost $70 billion in funding for CBP and ICE, as well as DHS overall.” [13] The money is “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1] and remains available “until September 30, 2029” [1]. The package comes “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [14]

points.title: It adds capacity for enforcement that targets people by ethnic or national background.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It adds capacity for enforcement that targets people by ethnic or national background.

  • Because S.2 funds CBP staff and operations “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Human Rights Watch documented ICE and CBP tactics in Los Angeles in summer 2025 that included “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [14].
  • So More capacity for these operations, without the reforms described above, increases exposure to this documented practice of treating groups as suspect.
  • So Accepting different ethnic and national groups gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for treating their background as grounds for suspicion.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect the added staffing to increased ethnic profiling under the conditions in place at the vote.

  • Because Section 201 funds “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1]. That includes salaries and training as well as hiring; it does not identify the methods used in added operations.
  • Because The investigation describes a particular campaign “throughout the summer of 2025 in Los Angeles” [14]. The relevant forecast concerns added work after June 9, 2026.
  • Because Before the vote, CBS reported a change in Border Patrol's street operations, according to border czar Tom Homan: “He noted that, since the Minneapolis operation was scaled back, Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [15]
  • So The PRO projects the earlier campaign's methods onto added staffing without addressing this later change in operations. More enforcement capacity does not establish increased exposure to that particular method of selecting people.

points.title: It funds the separation of established immigrant neighbors from their families and communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It funds the separation of established immigrant neighbors from their families and communities.

  • Because S.2 pays for “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because A report published before the vote found: “Individuals who are not public safety threats and have deep ties to their communities have been indiscriminately targeted under this administration.” [16] It also records children experiencing “family separation as a result of a parent being detained.” [16]
  • Because The bill sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” [1] for specified immigration arrest and custody work, including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens” [1].
  • Because Some adults qualify without a conviction: “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” [1].
  • Because This arrest fund cannot pay for release or community alternatives unless existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” [1].
  • So The added deportation funding and the arrest fund's preference for custody strengthen the means of separating people from community life, including parents and people without convictions.
  • So Accepting different people as neighbors gives [NAME] a reason to oppose greater capacity to exclude the non-threatening, established community members described above.
points.con_html:
Response Separation from family and the absence of a conviction do not by themselves establish rejection of people for being different.

  • Because The transportation provision funds “alien departure or removal operations.” [1] Removal is a civil process tied to immigration status: “deportation is classified as a civil rather than a criminal sanction” [17].
  • Because The arrest fund's category includes an adult who, “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” [1]. These are criminal-process and immigration-custody conditions, not tests of ethnicity, faith, or opinion.
  • Because The release-spending restriction applies to “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” [1] and retains the exception “except as required by existing law” [1]. It does not itself cancel release rights or bar other funding for release.
  • So The PRO identifies family disruption and a preference for custody. Neither makes acceptance of someone's background or beliefs depend on preserving their residence. The missing value link is why enforcing these civil rules rejects difference; the absence of a conviction does not supply it.

points.title: It expands the police role that leads Latino residents to withdraw from contact and community life.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It expands the police role that leads Latino residents to withdraw from contact and community life.

  • Because S.2 funds “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. These are “agreements that allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” [18].
  • Because A 2012 survey of Latinos in four counties found reluctance to contact police “specifically because they fear that police officers will inquire about the immigration status of themselves, their friends, or their family members.” [19]
  • Because The same survey found: “Many Latinos feel isolated and admit to withdrawing from their community.” [19]
  • Because This withdrawal also appears in recent reporting. In March 2025, CalMatters reported a volunteer's account that “some families have refused to leave the house for fear of apprehension by immigration enforcement agents.” [20]
  • So Expanding the immigration role of local police strengthens a reason residents give for avoiding contact. The harm reaches beyond those detained: fear keeps other neighbors apart.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a reason to oppose this added barrier to everyday contact.
points.con_html:
Response The evidence does not establish the added social withdrawal attributed to S.2's expansion of local police agreements.

  • Because The survey collected answers “during the period November 17 to December 10, 2012.” [19] Its isolation measure includes the statement “I feel more isolated because local law enforcement is more involved in immigration enforcement” [19]. That records respondents' views about policing; it does not compare changes following expansion of the agreements S.2 funds.
  • Because Those agreements cover different kinds of work. ICE describes its Warrant Service Officer model as authorizing local officers “to execute civil immigration warrants on behalf of ERO.” [21] The document concerns warrants served on people already in custody, rather than new street questioning.
  • Because The recent article concerns federal raids and rumors, including instances when “volunteers show up to a report of a raid, only to find the rumors were prank calls.” [20] It also reports: “The sheriff has previously insisted in a video message that his office does not enforce federal immigration law.” [20]
  • So A survey about police involvement generally and an account of fear where the sheriff disclaims that role do not establish the effect of adding these agreements. The PRO leaves out which added police contacts would produce the claimed barrier to community life.

points.title: It gives more legal help to the side seeking deportation while immigrants face barriers to presenting their own circumstances.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It gives more legal help to the side seeking deportation while immigrants face barriers to presenting their own circumstances.

  • Because S.2 funds government lawyers “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” [1]
  • Because The American Immigration Council explains the existing imbalance: “Yet, in every immigration case, the government is represented by a trained attorney who can argue for deportation, regardless of whether the immigrant is represented.” [17]
  • Because The same report explains why detention hinders an immigrant's answer: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” [17]
  • Because A detention inspection described before the vote found “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.” [16]
  • So The bill directs added legal help toward the case for deportation in a system where people in custody face documented barriers to presenting their own case.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to hear and understand those people gives a reason to oppose that spending priority.
points.con_html:
Response Directing money to government lawyers does not itself show a choice against hearing immigrants' circumstances.

  • Because Listening to someone's circumstances does not require agreeing that they should win their legal case.
  • Because Their funded role is “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” [1] The existing system already provides that representation: “in every immigration case, the government is represented by a trained attorney who can argue for deportation, regardless of whether the immigrant is represented.” [17]
  • Because The report locates immigrants' communication barriers in detention: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” [17] That does not describe an effect of hiring government lawyers.
  • Because The government's lawyer does not decide whose account prevails. The same report explains: “If the Notice to Appear does not state a valid ground for removal, the judge must terminate the case.” [17]
  • So The PRO establishes a need for immigrants' legal help. It does not establish that funding the other party rejects their account or blocks its presentation. The unequal spending priority becomes an argument about tolerance only by assuming that support for the government's case works against listening to immigrants.

points.title: It funds operations with a record of using force against peaceful opponents and people reporting on them.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It funds operations with a record of using force against peaceful opponents and people reporting on them.

  • Because S.2 pays for ICE's “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]
  • Because Human Rights Watch's October 2025 investigation documented “excessive force against peaceful protesters, legal observers, volunteer street medics, and journalists” [22] outside the Broadview, Illinois, detention facility.
  • Because Its findings rest on witnesses and video: “Witnesses and video confirm that DHS agents used tear gas and fired projectiles directly into groups of protesters, including from the detention facility roof, often without warning, and without protesters appearing to pose any risk to agents.” [22]
  • So Added operating funds without the reforms described above support enforcement with a documented pattern of intimidating peaceful critics and those who help others hear their views.
  • So Accepting people who disagree gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for that intimidation.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's forecast of added intimidation leaves out changes in the operations and command that produced the cited confrontations.

  • Because Human Rights Watch tied the Broadview escalation to Operation Midway Blitz and “an increase in immigration raids and seizures throughout the Chicago area.” [22]
  • Because Before the vote, CBS reported: “Earlier this year, Mr. Trump charged Homan with winding down the Minneapolis operation after the fatal shootings of U.S. citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Good by federal immigration agents sparked intense, bipartisan backlash.” [15]
  • Because CBS also reported a change in the command behind the city sweeps: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [15]
  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1] That provision does not direct a return to the earlier city-sweep approach.
  • So The PRO uses confrontations during an earlier approach to forecast the added operating work without addressing changes made before the vote. The earlier record does not establish that S.2 extends that way of confronting peaceful critics.

points.title: It supports surveillance used to make criticism of immigration enforcement personally threatening.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It supports surveillance used to make criticism of immigration enforcement personally threatening.

  • Because S.2 funds “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations” [1].
  • Because The Brennan Center's analysis connects this funding to broader surveillance: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [23]
  • Because In March 2026, NPR reported: “Activists and journalists spoke of tactics they felt were intimidating: agents photographing their faces or license plates; calling them by name; or leading them to their homes.” [24]
  • Because NPR withheld one observer's last name because “she fears retaliation from the federal government for speaking out.” [24]
  • So The added capacity supports surveillance with a documented use against critics and a documented fear of retaliation for speaking. That puts pressure on people to conceal their voices.
  • So [NAME]'s acceptance of disagreement gives a reason to oppose extending this pressure on peaceful expression.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not trace its examples of personal intimidation to the technology spending S.2 adds.

  • Because The provision covers “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations, including improvements to fee collections and body-worn cameras.” [1] Its scope is broader than tools for identifying critics.
  • Because NPR leaves the data source in the name-and-address encounters unresolved. It reports that “privacy advocates say federal agents may be running license plates to access Department of Motor Vehicle data” [24]. That does not establish which added resources these encounters depend on.
  • Because Brennan predicts that the funding will support “surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [23] That prediction concerns collecting information; the further claim concerns agents using it to threaten peaceful critics.
  • So The PRO joins a broad collection forecast to encounters whose data source is unidentified. It does not establish which added capability sustains the intimidation, or how maintaining enforcement systems increases the pressure to hide one's views.

points.title: It funds detention where minority religious practice is blocked.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It funds detention where minority religious practice is blocked.

  • Because S.2 funds “facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Washington's Department of Health reported in April 2026: “DOH has seen an increase in complaints regarding lack of access to religious services, prayer, and religious diets during Ramadan 2026.” [25]
  • Because A March 2026 report describes a Muslim detainee's request to pray with others: “Vijandre has asked the facility’s chaplain for a quieter place and permission to pray with the dozens of other Muslim detainees in their housing unit. The chaplain tried to help, but Vijandre said he learned the warden denied the request.” [26]
  • So Added support for detention without the reforms described above helps keep centers running with current, documented barriers to minority worship.
  • So Accepting different religious groups gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added funding for holding people under conditions that block their faith.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Reported worship barriers include a warden's decision and complaints that do not mention funding. The 2025 law funded detention through FY2029. Sources: [25], [26], [27].

pages.description: S.2 provides about $70 billion through 2029 for immigration enforcement and border security. It increases the number of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers; expands resources for detention and deportation operations; invests in border security technology; and supports other federal immigration enforcement activities.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.2 adds money for existing border protection, criminal investigations, and immigration enforcement through September 2029. Its appropriations are “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1] and “to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1]. Section 102’s investigation funds cover work outside immigration and customs enforcement: “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]

points.title: Added drug scanners strengthen protection against fentanyl poisoning.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Added drug scanners strengthen protection against fentanyl poisoning.

  • Because Section 103 funds new scanners and drug interception: “Procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment” [1] and “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1].
  • Because Scanners have helped uncover hidden fentanyl. In a 2024 vehicle inspection, “CBP officers used non-intrusive technology to screen the sedan revealing anomalies inside all four tires of the vehicle.” [2] Officers recovered packages from the tires: “Four of the packages contained nearly 54,000 blue fentanyl pills” [2].
  • Because These drugs pose a hidden, lethal health risk: “Drugs may contain deadly levels of fentanyl, and you wouldn't be able to see it, taste it, or smell it.” [3]
  • So Finding and seizing concealed drug loads keeps those drugs out of circulation. Funding more of this work strengthens protection against a poison in the U.S. drug supply, serving [NAME]’s wish to protect their health.
points.con_html:
Response A successful seizure does not establish the drop in fentanyl exposure that the PRO attributes to more scanners.

  • Because Section 103 funds “Procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment” [1]. Equipment purchases and usable scanning capacity are different: GAO’s January 2026 review reports, “Some factors have limited the use of the systems, such as limited staff and system outages.” [4]
  • Because Seized fentanyl can be replaced. Jonathan Caulkins explains that synthetic opioids “permit seizures to be replaced in days” [5]. The number seized does not show how much less fentanyl buyers can obtain.
  • So The PRO leaves two links unsupported: how this funding adds usable scanning beyond existing resources, and how added seizures reduce consumers’ exposure after suppliers respond. Its seized-pill example does not establish the added health protection.

points.title: Added funding for criminal investigations strengthens protection against poisoned pills sold as real medicine.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Added funding for criminal investigations strengthens protection against poisoned pills sold as real medicine.

  • Because Section 102 funds Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), ICE’s criminal investigation branch: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI and its partners have investigated fake pharmacies selling pills made in U.S. drug factories. Their report describes the seizure of pills from those factories: “Law enforcement raided at least three of these pill mills and two other narcotics storage locations, seizing approximately 625,000 counterfeit pills” [6].
  • Because This fraud reaches people seeking health care. The report describes victims “who were in need of medication — people suffering with legitimate ailments.” [6] It reports, “At least nine of the victims later died of narcotics poisoning.” [6]
  • So Added funding supports finding these sellers and removing their poisoned pills from sale. That protects people seeking medicine, giving [NAME] a health reason to favor this added capacity.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect its pharmacy case to work that Section 102’s restricted funds may pay for.

  • Because The money must support “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1] Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is the criminal investigation branch cited by the PRO; not every HSI activity is an allowed use of this money.
  • Because The case concerns an international drug operation: “Lopez Reyes led the enterprise, orchestrating and controlling every facet of the scheme from the Dominican Republic.” [6] The report also says “the defendants shipped counterfeit pharmaceuticals to victims across the United States and around the world” [6].
  • So Locating pill factories in U.S. basements does not place the investigation outside customs work. The PRO identifies no part of this international case that the restricted funds would expand outside the excluded missions.

points.title: More capacity to hold and remove convicted violent offenders limits their opportunities for further attacks.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 More capacity to hold and remove convicted violent offenders limits their opportunities for further attacks.

  • Because Section 202 funds enforcement staff and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because This work includes custody after a criminal sentence ends. ICE reported that it “apprehended an illegally present Dominican national convicted for murder in Massachusetts in 2007 when officers arrested Cesar Augusto Polanco, 59, January 24 at the Massachusetts Correctional Institution in Norfolk after he was released from state custody.” [7]
  • Because ICE kept him in custody for the removal process: “Polanco remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” [7]
  • So Holding convicted violent offenders after prison release, and carrying out their removal, separates them from people they could attack here. Added funding for staff and transport backs that protection for U.S. residents such as [NAME].
points.con_html:
Response One existing detention does not establish that S.2’s broader removal funding reduces residents’ exposure to violence.

  • Because The February 2025 report says, “Polanco remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” [7] That report documents custody achieved before S.2, not a detention that depends on it.
  • Because Existing law already supplied detention funding. CRS lists the 2025 law’s “$45 billion for detention capacity” [8]. The PRO does not show that S.2’s added staff and transport would prevent a loss of custody or hold a violent offender who would otherwise be released.
  • Because Research on a comparable detention-and-deportation program found, “The results show that the Secure Communities program has had no observable effect on the overall crime rate.” [9] A separate study of violent victimization in 2005–2014 reports, “The activation of 287(g) jail enforcement agreements and anti-detainer policies had no significant impact on violent victimization risk during the period.” [10]
  • So The example establishes an existing separation from the public. The broader studies do not supply the missing evidence that this additional removal funding reduces violence; the PRO cannot infer that result from the single detention.

points.title: Supporting transfers from jails makes safer arrests possible.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Supporting transfers from jails makes safer arrests possible.

  • Because Section 202 funds partnerships with state and local police: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act” [1].
  • Because One form of these agreements lets trained local officers identify people in jail for immigration proceedings. ICE explains that they “place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.” [11]
  • Because A transfer can avoid a dangerous arrest in public. In the Polanco case, ICE said cooperation let officers “make the arrest in the safety of a jail cell rather than sending a team of officers into the community to make a potentially dangerous arrest.” [7]
  • So Funding these partnerships supports more arrests in controlled settings. Keeping those confrontations out of public places protects nearby residents, giving [NAME] a separate reason grounded in personal safety.
points.con_html:
Response Expanding 287(g) agreements does not establish that public arrests would be replaced by jail transfers.

  • Because The cited transfer already occurred through cooperation: “The Massachusetts Correctional Institution honored the immigration detainer and informed ICE Boston of Polanco’s release.” [7]
  • Because These agreements give local officers some immigration powers, including outside jails. ICE’s February 2026 description says, “The Task Force Model allows your officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.” [12]
  • Because Section 202 funds agreements generally. It also funds “release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” [1]. It does not direct officers to replace public arrests with jail transfers.
  • So More authority to make immigration arrests is different from moving the same arrests into jails. The PRO’s example shows the safety of an existing transfer, not a change in arrest setting caused by S.2.

points.title: Funding trafficking investigations strengthens protection against forced work and sexual violence.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Funding trafficking investigations strengthens protection against forced work and sexual violence.

  • Because Section 102 pays for HSI agents and support staff, including “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. DHS says HSI “conducts criminal human trafficking investigations worldwide.” [13]
  • Because Trafficking is a danger within U.S. life: “many human traffickers and victims are U.S. citizens.” [13] Contact can begin through ordinary relationships or job searches: “They can be relatives, romantic partners, or close family friends. Or they can be the people behind an employment ad or a new friend on social media or online gaming.” [13]
  • Because Traffickers’ control includes “actual physical assaults and sexual violence” [13]. Identifying victims also opens a route to help, including “medical and mental health care, safety planning, and legal services” [13].
  • So Added funding supports identifying violent exploitation and bringing victims into protection and care. Protection against abuse through everyday work and relationships serves the personal safety [NAME] values.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: GAO (2016) says trafficking is hard to distinguish from other crimes and victims may be unwilling to testify. Referrals follow identification. SEP's brief carries no reassignment evidence. Sources: [14], [13].

points.title: Stronger gang investigations protect people from violence in their communities.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Stronger gang investigations protect people from violence in their communities.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents “to hire, pay, train, and equip” [1]. Section 203 also allows support for state and local crime prevention through “paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21” [1]; paragraph (7) includes “addressing crime and public safety threats” [15].
  • Because HSI has helped investigate gang violence that led to convictions. A Justice Department report says “the defendants were also convicted of conspiring with each other and committing acts of violence” [16], and identifies the investigators: “The ATF, HSI, DEA, U.S. Marshals Service, Metropolitan Nashville Police Department, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, La Vergne Police Department, and Kentucky State Police investigated the case.” [16]
  • Because The danger extends to ordinary residents: “Throughout the course of the conspiracy, the MS-13 members committed several armed carjackings of citizens near the Nashville, Tennessee, area.” [16]
  • So Funding federal investigators and local partners strengthens the ability to investigate and prosecute violent gangs. Disrupting their attacks protects [NAME]’s safety while moving through the community.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: §203's $2.5 billion may go to a menu of uses already funded by the 2025 law, and the cited MS-13 case closed in July 2024. The reviewed record does not identify an allocation of S.2 funds to local gang prevention. Sources: [1], [15], [16].

points.title: Funding border checks strengthens screening for terrorism threats before entry or release.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Funding border checks strengthens screening for terrorism threats before entry or release.

  • Because Section 201 funds border agents and support staff “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Border Patrol uses names, photographs, and fingerprints in these checks. Its inspector general reports: “The e3 Portal captures biographical information, photos, and fingerprints and automatically compares them to a series of Federal law enforcement databases that provide real-time potential criminal history information, including wants, warrant data, and terrorist watchlist matches.” [17]
  • Because The checks inform release decisions: “We determined that Border Patrol agents conducted required record checks and verified the checks did not contain derogatory information before releasing the migrants from our sample.” [17]
  • So Paying and equipping agents supports a screen for security threats before people enter U.S. communities. That protection against terrorism serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid danger.
points.con_html:
Response The reported end of releases narrows the PRO's release-screening example.

  • Because The inspector general found that agents completed record checks before releasing migrants in its sample. That 2022 audit describes how the screen worked then. [17]
  • Because A June 9 congressional press release says CBP had announced in May “a full year of zero releases at the border.” [18] This is an attributed account, not an independently verified measure of every encounter or route into the country.
  • So The older release audit does not establish the role of that particular route under the reported policy at the comparison date. This response is partial: it does not answer the case for sustaining checks at encounter or before entry, or show that added staffing cannot support those checks.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A June 9 congressional press release attributes a full year of zero border releases to CBP. This concerns the release route more directly than screening at encounter or before entry. The reviewed record does not independently establish all release or entry practices, or show that maintaining the screening system has no value. Sources: [18], [17].

points.title: Supporting existing border health duties strengthens protection against infectious disease.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Supporting existing border health duties strengthens protection against infectious disease.

  • Because Section 101 pays Border Patrol personnel for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1]
  • Because Border Patrol had an “immediate requirement to assist the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in implementing its May 18, 2026 Order” [19], with guidance on “screening, processing, and expulsion procedures under Title 42 authority.” [19] These are duties under public health law.
  • Because The May 18 order’s stated term covered June 9: “This order will be in effect for 30 days, effective immediately.” [20] CDC described its goal as “preventing its introduction into the United States.” [20] It explains the danger: “Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids and can be fatal.” [21]
  • Because CDC issued a continuing order on June 21, effective at 5:00 p.m. that day through July 21, and asked the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to help enforce it. This later evidence shows that DHS's supporting role continued beyond the May order's stated term. It does not name Border Patrol, establish uninterrupted coverage between the orders, or settle whether this work is payable under Section 101. [22]
  • So Funding personnel who carry out these existing health safeguards backs efforts to keep infection from reaching U.S. communities while the health orders apply. [NAME]’s wish to avoid disease gives [NAME] a reason to support that added backing.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence limitation: The May CBP account assigns Border Patrol a Title 42 supporting role. The June CDC order requests DHS help and names customs officers and the Coast Guard. It does not classify §101 spending. Would Border Patrol assistance implementing the public-health orders qualify under §101, its immigration/customs exclusion, or another eligible provision? Sources: [1], [19], [22].

points.title: Better aircraft and boats strengthen lifesaving rescue capacity.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Better aircraft and boats strengthen lifesaving rescue capacity.

  • Because Section 103 funds “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]
  • Because These crews use their boats and aircraft to rescue people. A report describes a Rochester boat crew finding a person in distress: “Agents rescued that person, observed signs of hypothermia, and provided medical attention.” [23]
  • Because Aircraft also reach stranded people. After finding people beside a capsized boat in Montana, a pilot “landed on a nearby sandbar, assessed the condition of two people, and loaded them into the helicopter.” [23]
  • So Better aircraft and boats add means to reach people in emergencies and bring them to safety. That serves [NAME]’s interest in surviving accidents and getting help when in danger.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 2025 law provided $6.168 billion across listed uses including the same platform purpose. The cited rescues date from 2023. No added deployment is identified. Sources: [15], [23].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 would give Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) an extra $31.075 billion for immigration enforcement and removal. Section 202 provides “$31,075,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1], “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]. This pays for more arrests, removals and work with local police. Human Rights Watch reports that Congress approved the funding “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [24]

points.title: More enforcement operations expose people going about daily life to violence by agents.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 More enforcement operations expose people going about daily life to violence by agents.

  • Because Section 202 pays for more enforcement staff: “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel and the personnel for all its directorates, including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Citizens have suffered physical harm: “Americans have been dragged, tackled, beaten, tased and shot by immigration agents.” [25]
  • Because People can be caught up while doing ordinary things. ProPublica reports that “agents grabbed and handcuffed a woman on her way to work who was caught up in a chaotic raid on street vendors.” [25]
  • So More operations using these practices create more chances for dangerous encounters during work and travel. [NAME]'s wish to avoid injury or death gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added exposure.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO assumes added enforcement would repeat the street practices behind its injury reports, despite a change in enforcement before June 9.

  • Because ProPublica links rising citizen detentions to a particular approach: “large-scale immigration sweeps across the country, often in communities that do not want them.” [25]
  • Because On May 1, the Associated Press reported a shift “away from aggressive, public-facing tactics toward a quieter approach to enforcement.” [26] It also reported that “there have been no new high-profile city-based operations launched” [26].
  • Because Section 202 pays for “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping” [1] personnel, including “attorneys and support staff” [1]. Those uses do not identify the tactics or settings of the added operations.
  • So The 2025 incident list does not establish how S.2 changes dangerous encounters under the later approach. The missing link is why the added operations would spread the practices that caused those injuries.

points.title: More arrests and custody expose citizens to confinement without needed medical care.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 More arrests and custody expose citizens to confinement without needed medical care.

  • Because S.2 supports custody as well as arrests: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Citizenship does not keep people out of this system: “We found more than 50 Americans who were held after agents questioned their citizenship.” [25]
  • Because Neglect is a wider custody problem. Human Rights Watch documented Florida detention conditions in 2025 that included “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” [24].
  • Because Medical neglect has reached citizens. A detained car wash owner's lawyer said “he was held for 12 hours and wasn’t given medical attention despite having broken ribs in the incident and having recently had heart surgery.” [25]
  • So Funding more arrests and custody expands exposure to a system where even citizens have been denied urgent care. Avoiding that danger to health and personal safety gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the funding.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 2025 law provided $45 billion for detention capacity. KFF attributes custody risk to compliance, health-care, staffing and oversight failures. The reviewed record does not identify an estimate of citizen detentions added by S.2. Sources: [27], [28].

points.title: Expanding local police immigration work weakens the crime reporting that protects the public.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Expanding local police immigration work weakens the crime reporting that protects the public.

  • Because S.2 funds 287(g) agreements, which let local police perform immigration enforcement: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)).” [1]
  • Because The program again includes a street-policing version, called the task force model: “Allows officers trained by ICE to enforce immigration law during routine police activity, like traffic stops.” [29]
  • Because A study using national crime-victim survey data from 2005–2014 found a higher risk of becoming a victim of violent crime: “the activation of Secure Communities and 287(g) task force agreements significantly increased violent victimization risk among Latinos” [10].
  • Because The reporting problem also weakens police protection for the wider public. The president of the Major Cities Chiefs Association explained: “Whether we seek to stop child predators, drug dealers, rapists or robbers – we need the full cooperation of victims and witness. Cooperation is not forthcoming from persons who see their police as immigration agents.” [30]
  • Because A February–March 2026 probability survey of Minneapolis and St. Paul adults asked about Operation Metro Surge, a large federal immigration deployment. In Minneapolis 49.4% and in St. Paul 46.1% agreed that they were less likely to seek help from law enforcement because of how ICE and Border Patrol agents conducted it. These are reported intentions about a federal operation, not measured crime outcomes or an effect of local police working under 287(g). [31]
  • So Paying to expand this police role expands a barrier to reporting crime and helping investigations. [NAME] relies on police being able to identify and stop dangerous offenders, so this loss of cooperation gives [NAME] a personal safety reason to oppose S.2.
points.con_html:
Response The evidence supports a help-seeking concern but does not identify which added local agreements cause a wider loss of protection.

  • Because S.2 funds local police immigration work through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1], without choosing between street policing and checks inside jails.
  • Because The older study reports that “our results for 287(g) jail programs showed no significant association with violent victimization risk” [10]. Its street-policing and Secure Communities results showed “no evident impact on victimization risk among non-Latino Whites and Blacks.” [10]
  • Because The study cannot distinguish reduced trust from other explanations: “The data assembled for our study cannot discern between these potential explanations.” [10] The newer Twin Cities survey reports reduced willingness to seek police help across adult residents, but it concerns federal agents' conduct during a large surge, ended fieldwork in March, and does not isolate local police, 287(g) or actual reporting. [31]
  • So These limits narrow the inference from older victimization results and federal-surge intentions to added local agreements. They do not answer the help-seeking concern itself or establish that only Latinos could be affected.

points.title: Expanded enforcement gives violent criminals more cover to pose as immigration agents.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Expanded enforcement gives violent criminals more cover to pose as immigration agents.

  • Because The FBI has documented the danger: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” [32].
  • Because Its bulletin connects that danger to enforcement's greater visibility. WIRED reports that “criminals are using Immigration and Custom Enforcement’s heightened profile to target vulnerable communities, making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.” [32]
  • Because S.2 leaves masked operations in place: “The GOP bill does not restrict mask-wearing” [33].
  • So More operations in this form give impersonators more of the cover they already exploit and make fake arrests harder to recognize. Avoiding robbery, kidnapping and assault gives [NAME] a safety reason to oppose this expansion.
points.con_html:
Response The FBI's warning rests partly on public visibility, which had reportedly fallen before S.2, and the mask provision marks no change.

  • Because WIRED reports that criminals use ICE's “heightened profile to target vulnerable communities, making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.” [32] The same report links the rise in these crimes to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [32].
  • Because Before S.2, the Associated Press reported a move toward “a quieter approach to enforcement.” [26] It also reported that “ICE arrests have fallen in recent months” [26]. More enforcement work and a higher public profile are different changes.
  • Because The mask provision cited by the PRO is an absence of reform: “The GOP bill does not restrict mask-wearing” [33]. It does not introduce the practice.
  • So A public profile from the earlier period may not carry over to quieter operations, and keeping an existing mask practice does not itself create extra cover. This narrows the PRO to the link between enforcement actions and impersonation. It does not show that added operations would create no further cover.

points.title: More enforcement and removals threaten the supply of care when Americans need it.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 More enforcement and removals threaten the supply of care when Americans need it.

  • Because S.2 pays for deportations: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Past enforcement reduced nursing care. A study comparing counties as Secure Communities began found that “the program reduced directcare staff hours per resident day” [34]. These are hours of hands-on care in nursing homes.
  • Because Another study of that program's 2008–2013 rollout found both fewer home care workers and less help for older adults: “We find that Secure Communities reduces the overall size of the home care workforce by 7.5%” [35]; “older adults needing assistance are 2.9 percentage points less likely to receive any help at home” [35].
  • Because Among Twin Cities survey respondents who missed work over enforcement concerns, about 28% reported a caregiver unable to attend. This is a local self-report about disrupted care, not a decline in the national care workforce. [31]
  • So S.2 pays to expand local immigration checks, arrests and removals. The earlier rollout and contemporary reports support a risk to care availability. They do not estimate how much S.2 would add to that risk.
  • Because This is an ordinary lifetime health need: “Most Americans will need long-term care at some point in their lifetimes” [35].
  • Because Shortages also threaten hospital care. JAMA explains: “The resulting shortages could reverberate through emergency departments and hospitals, leading to the inability to discharge patients and tying up nurses and other staff.” [36]
  • So [NAME] depends on timely care, whether at home, in a nursing home or in a hospital. Protecting access to that care gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose the added enforcement funding.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: KFF found health-care employment rose about 1% from January 2025 to April 2026, with noncitizen workers up (961,000 to 1.2 million) and naturalized workers down (2.5 to 2.3 million), while noncitizen workers overall fell about 4%. Immigrants were 30% of direct long-term-care workers in 2024. The rollout studies measure starting Secure Communities in 2008–2013. The Twin Cities caregiver figures are 28.7% and 27.8% of respondents who missed work. The targeted search did not find a local staffing series that resolves Q21. Sources: [1], [37], [31], [34], [35], [27].

points.title: More enforcement around health care obstructs disease detection and treatment for the community.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 More enforcement around health care obstructs disease detection and treatment for the community.

  • Because Enforcement already reaches medical settings: “The Infectious Diseases Society of America is alarmed by reports of immigration enforcement activity occurring near health care settings.” [38]
  • Because S.2 expands enforcement without adding hospital protections: “It does not stop raids at daycares, churches, or even hospitals.” [39]
  • Because Clinicians explain how this discourages care: “When patients fear that seeking care could expose them or their loved ones to immigration enforcement, they delay or avoid treatment, disengage from therapeutic care, decline crisis services, and withhold clinically relevant information.” [40]
  • Because In the 2026 Twin Cities survey, 29.2% of Minneapolis respondents with scheduled appointments and 20.6% in St. Paul reported missing one because of enforcement concerns. This is contemporary self-report, not an estimate of S.2’s additional effect. [31]
  • Because Infectious disease specialists identify the wider health risk: “Fear of seeking health care puts individual patients at risk and threatens the health of entire communities, including by delaying the timely identification and treatment of infectious diseases.” [38]
  • So Expanding enforcement around these services adds barriers to finding and treating infections. [NAME] shares the community's exposure to contagious disease, so protecting disease control gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose S.2.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

points.title: Supporting more detention sustains a route for infections to reach the wider public.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Supporting more detention sustains a route for infections to reach the wider public.

  • Because S.2 pays to keep enforcement facilities operating: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because KFF reports “recent measles outbreaks in Arizona and Texas detention facilities” [28] and explains: “Overcrowding as well as limited capacity and resources may also increase the risk of the spread of communicable diseases, such as measles.” [28]
  • Because Outbreaks have infected people outside the detained population. In its report on the 2018–2019 mumps outbreaks in migrant detention facilities, CDC recorded that “an additional 33 cases occurred among staff members.” [41]
  • Because Staff connect detention facilities to daily community life: “ICE detention facilities are often located in small, isolated towns that employ local residents who move each day between facility and community.” [42]
  • So More arrests feeding this system, and money to sustain it, increase opportunities for infections to reach the public through staff. [NAME]'s interest in avoiding disease gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added exposure.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that S.2 adds infectious contacts between detention staff and the wider public.

  • Because KFF's crowding warning depends on the balance between arrivals and departures: detention “can lead to overcrowding if deportations do not keep up with the pace of arrests” [28]. S.2 funds both facility upkeep and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because CDC's 2019 report records “an additional 33 cases occurred among staff members.” [41] It also records an actual response: “IHSC provided >25,000 doses of measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine in response to mumps in 56 facilities.” [41]
  • So More arrests do not by themselves establish greater crowding or fewer resources when the bill also funds departures and upkeep.
  • So The remaining step is added exposure for ordinary community members. Staff cases and daily commutes identify a possible route; they do not show that S.2 increases infectious contacts along it under the disease controls in use. The PRO treats support for detention as proof of that increase.

points.title: More enforcement spreads fear and mental health harm beyond the people detained.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 More enforcement spreads fear and mental health harm beyond the people detained.

  • Because Psychiatrists describe the link from enforcement fears to illness: “Fear of detention, deportation, or family separation acts as a chronic psychological stressor, contributing to anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, isolation from community support, and worsening of serious mental illness.” [40]
  • Because People need not be detained to suffer these effects: “Reports of violent encounters involving federal immigration agents, including recent fatal and non fatal shootings, intensify fear, psychological distress, and community-wide trauma.” [40]
  • So Funding more of these operations exposes the wider community to fear and trauma. [NAME]'s wish to protect mental health and be personally secure gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO extends distress in communities facing enforcement to [NAME] without establishing the exposure that makes its mental-health claim work.

  • Because The psychiatric statement identifies the stressor as “Fear of detention, deportation, or family separation” [40]. It also says reports of violent encounters “intensify fear, psychological distress, and community-wide trauma.” [40]
  • Because Its extension beyond patients concerns families and affected communities: “These harms extend beyond individual patients to families and communities, with children particularly vulnerable to the destabilizing effects of fear, uncertainty, and parental separation.” [40]
  • So Exposure can come through reports as well as direct encounters, but the PRO still must connect S.2's added enforcement to [NAME]'s fear or illness. Being outside detention does not establish that connection for an average American. Calling trauma community-wide does not fill the gap.

pages.description: S.2 provides about $70 billion through 2029 for immigration enforcement and border security. It increases the number of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers; expands resources for detention and deportation operations; invests in border security technology; and supports other federal immigration enforcement activities.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on June 9, 2026, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 adds $69.545 billion to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for border security, immigration enforcement, and related work: “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]; “TOTAL $69.545 billion” [2]. This adds to the 2025 law, which “included multi-year funding for several elements of DHS.” [2] The new funds remain available through September 2029: “to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1]. They include $7.45 billion for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the criminal investigation service within Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE): “$7,450,000,000” [1]. Section 102 limits that funding to “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1] The HSI reasons below concern its other criminal investigations and protective work.

points.title: It gives security agencies steadier resources to keep trained officers ready.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives security agencies steadier resources to keep trained officers ready.

  • Because The April 2026 annual funding law excluded Border Patrol and ICE: it “did not include funding for the U.S. Border Patrol or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement” [2].
  • Because An April 3 presidential directive had already told DHS to use funds with “a reasonable and logical nexus to the functions of DHS” to compensate employees during the lapse, “subject to the availability of appropriations.” S.2 therefore adds dedicated appropriations to a baseline with that lapse-period instruction; it does not create the first possible pay route. [3]
  • Because S.2 adds money available through September 2029 “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel” [1]. It also adds flexible funding that the administration describes as “$5 billion in additional appropriations to DHS to account for any unforeseen costs that ICE and Border Patrol may incur in future years” [4].
  • So Funding that carries across budget years, pays officers, and covers unexpected costs supports a ready security workforce. That serves [NAME]’s concern for a strong state able to defend people.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Baseline: P.L. 119-21 funds CBP hiring, training, retention and bonuses, and ICE operations, through FY2029; end-May unobligated balances were reported at $62 billion (ICE) and $33 billion (CBP) by Senate Budget minority staff. The April 3 directive told DHS to pay employees from funds with a nexus to its functions, subject to law and available appropriations. The reviewed record contains no employee-level pay audit. GAO reported attrition outpacing hiring for Border Patrol agents and a coming retirement surge. Steadiness is weakest for ICE. Size is unresolved (Q02, Q23). Sources: [1], [5], [2], [4], [3], [6], [7], [8].

points.title: It strengthens control over land and sea borders.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It strengthens control over land and sea borders.

  • Because It funds “Upgrades and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] It also funds new air and sea equipment for “rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]
  • Because It requires land-border towers to be tested for their ability to work on their own. It bars spending on towers that “have not been tested and accepted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1]
  • Because Existing towers show how detection leads to action: “These towers have been instrumental in identifying and tracking border crossings, contributing significantly to successful apprehensions in the sector.” [9]
  • Because Customs and Border Protection (CBP) says technology and equipment investments “increase agent safety” [10] and “improve CBP’s ability to respond to detected threats and other urgent situations” [10].
  • So Better detection, response equipment, and officer safety strengthen the ability to intercept crossings and smuggling. Control over U.S. territory directly serves [NAME]’s concern for a secure country.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: GAO (February 2026) found a northern-border staffing gap among specialists who monitor surveillance, with no plan to address it. The 2025 law provided $6.168 billion including border surveillance and has the same tower rule. Sources: [11], [6].

points.title: It makes identity and departure checks harder to evade.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It makes identity and departure checks harder to evade.

  • Because It funds identity checks based on physical traits, such as face images: “Necessary expenses, including the deployment of technology, relating to the biometric entry and exit system” [1].
  • Because CBP explains that its face-comparison service can “identify the traveler biometrically and to enable CBP to confirm and expedite the traveler’s arrival or departure.” [12]
  • Because CBP reports that “facial comparison results in better security by reducing imposter threats.” [12] It also uses departure checks for security: “CBP performs watchlist vetting of departing travelers.” [12]
  • So More reliable identity and departure checks make false identities harder to use and strengthen checks against security records. This supports the state’s ability to control who crosses its borders and detect threats.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish an improvement in identity checks or their coverage attributable to S.2.

  • Because CBP's March 2025 report already said it “has the capacity to support increased usage of CBP biometric matching service as more airlines participate.” [12] The July 2025 law then funded “Necessary expenses, including the deployment of technology, relating to the biometric entry and exit system” [6] within its border-technology budget.
  • Because Broader legal authority also predates S.2: “The final rule, effective Dec. 26, 2025, amends existing DHS regulations to authorize U.S. Customs and Border Protection” [13] to collect face images from noncitizens across travel modes.
  • Because Air-exit expansion also depends on airlines and airports choosing to join. CBP's requirements say participation “is voluntary and is not mandated by CBP.” [14]
  • So The matching service, permission to expand, and prior funding belong in the comparison with current law. Describing their security uses does not show that S.2 changes matching accuracy, partner participation, or action on watchlist hits.

points.title: It strengthens defenses against fentanyl and other dangerous drugs.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It strengthens defenses against fentanyl and other dangerous drugs.

  • Because It funds inspection equipment “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] Its purposes include fighting “fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1], the chemicals used to make it.
  • Because This equipment has intercepted drugs. In fiscal year 2023, CBP reported that large-scale scanning systems were “aiding in the interdiction of more than 127,000 pounds of narcotics” [10].
  • Because CBP explains the protective step: “Seizures remove dangerous drugs from illicit supply chains, keep them out of our communities, and deny TCOs valuable profits.” [10] TCOs are criminal groups operating across countries.
  • So More means to detect and intercept drugs strengthen protection against a lethal threat to U.S. communities, giving [NAME] a security reason to favor the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The past seizure total does not show that S.2 would turn equipment purchases into more effective drug inspections.

  • Because S.2 funds inspection equipment and “associated civil works” [1], meaning work to prepare sites. The remaining steps include sound deployment plans, trained operators, and reliable repairs.
  • Because The Department of Homeland Security's inspector general found that CBP “did not follow Department of Homeland Security acquisition policy, did not consider relevant information during planning, and did not have a well-defined maintenance and sustainment plan” [15]. These findings concerned purchases and operations before S.2.
  • Because GAO's January 2026 testimony reported that officials at all four field offices it visited “did not always have sufficient staff to fully use the systems.” [16]
  • So The PRO does not connect the added spending to usable inspections under those conditions. The weight of drugs seized by earlier systems cannot supply that missing connection.

points.title: It strengthens arrest and removal operations against people who threaten public safety.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It strengthens arrest and removal operations against people who threaten public safety.

  • Because It pays ICE personnel and funds “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because It sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” [1] for work including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” [1].
  • Because It also funds local cooperation: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. Under the jail version of these agreements, local officers help “identify criminal aliens and immigration violators in state and local custody and place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.” [17]
  • Because These tools reach people with serious criminal records. ICE’s 2024 arrests included charges and convictions for “sexual assault and sex offenses” [18] and “homicides” [18]. ICE explains the custody link: “When criminal noncitizens complete their sentences, ICE assumes custody and places them in the appropriate removal proceedings.” [18]
  • So More staff, custody transfers, and transport give ICE more means to keep removable violent offenders from returning to communities after prison and to carry out their removal. That strengthens public protection, which [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that the broader arrest and removal funding would add protection from violent offenders.

  • Because The $350 million provision covers people after “an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense” [1]. A violent conviction is not required.
  • Because The 2025 law already funded removal transport: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [6] It also funded expansion of 287(g) agreements, which let local police perform immigration duties: “Expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [6].
  • Because A federally funded study using 2005–2010 data on 287(g) applicants concluded: “We find no evidence that these 287(g) arrangements had meaningful crime reduction benefits.” [19]
  • So Serious offenses among earlier ICE arrests do not establish the effect of expanding these broader operations. The study weighs against assuming that more immigration enforcement means less violence.

points.title: It strengthens criminal cases against terrorists and violent gangs.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It strengthens criminal cases against terrorists and violent gangs.

  • Because Section 102 funds staff “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI builds criminal cases against “terrorist networks and facilitators” [20], including the people who help those networks operate.
  • Because HSI also pursues violent gangs. Its 2024 report describes gang cases involving “firearms trafficking and possession, violent crimes, terroristic acts” [18] and reports that gang investigations produced “2,189 indictments and 1,106 convictions.” [18]
  • So Funding investigators who build these cases strengthens the state’s ability to disrupt organized violence and terrorism. That directly serves [NAME]’s concern that the United States defend itself against threats.
points.con_html:
Response Past terrorism and gang cases by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) do not establish that S.2 would put more investigators on those cases.

  • Because A January 2026 Senate letter reported that agents had been taken off criminal cases. It said a joint FBI-HSI investigation into suspected terrorist financing through Iranian oil shipments “has suffered from the redeployment” [21].
  • Because Section 102 funds HSI's general staff and “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. It assigns no added terrorism or gang team.
  • So The PRO's historical cases do not establish the claimed change in investigators available for those cases under the later assignment policy.

Shared objection Reported changes in HSI assignments weaken the inference from a larger general HSI budget to more investigators or officers available for the criminal investigations and protective work in these points.

  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement. This is the same assignment evidence cited in the point-specific responses; it is not a finding about the future assignments of Section 102 hires.
  • Because Section 102's limit governs “funds provided in this section” [1]. Section 202 separately pays personnel across “all its directorates” [1] “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • So Section 102 restricts how its own money may be used. It does not settle how staff paid from other funds will be assigned under the reported priorities. The assignment evidence gives a reason to question whether added capacity reaches the named work; it does not show that it cannot, or that Section 102 hires would be reassigned.

points.title: It strengthens protection against sex trafficking and forced labor.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It strengthens protection against sex trafficking and forced labor.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI investigators and “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because HSI’s work includes criminal cases against people who force adults into sex or work. In a 2025 Delaware case, a jury convicted a trafficker on “seven counts of sex trafficking seven adult victims, five counts of forced labor, and one count of interstate transportation for purposes of prostitution.” [22] The Justice Department states: “Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.” [22]
  • So Supporting this work gives the state more means to stop coercion and abuse within U.S. communities. Protecting people from organized predatory crime serves [NAME]’s concern for a secure country.
points.con_html:
Response The trafficking conviction does not establish that S.2 would expand the staff doing trafficking investigations.

  • Because Cato's September 2025 account reported that HSI “is suspending investigations into human trafficking, child exploitation, cybercrime, weapons export controls, intellectual property theft, drugs, and terrorism to focus on arresting immigrants.” [23]
  • Because Section 102 allows spending on “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1], without directing a larger trafficking team.
  • So The conviction shows the result of an investigation. It does not show that the added money would reach such work under the assignments Cato describes.

Shared objection Reported changes in HSI assignments weaken the inference from a larger general HSI budget to more investigators or officers available for the criminal investigations and protective work in these points.

  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement. This is the same assignment evidence cited in the point-specific responses; it is not a finding about the future assignments of Section 102 hires.
  • Because Section 102's limit governs “funds provided in this section” [1]. Section 202 separately pays personnel across “all its directorates” [1] “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • So Section 102 restricts how its own money may be used. It does not settle how staff paid from other funds will be assigned under the reported priorities. The assignment evidence gives a reason to question whether added capacity reaches the named work; it does not show that it cannot, or that Section 102 hires would be reassigned.

points.title: It directly expands the ability to find and rescue sexually exploited children.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It directly expands the ability to find and rescue sexually exploited children.

  • Because It dedicates “$108,500,000” [1] to staff who investigate abuse and examine evidence: “shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” [1].
  • Because Their task is “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1]. The funding also trains federal, state, and local staff: “to train such personnel and State and local law enforcement regarding identifying victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1].
  • Because This work reaches children in the United States. In 2024 testimony about online sexual blackmail, HSI reported that it “has identified and rescued over 675 domestic victims of West Africa-based sextortion schemes.” [20]
  • So Additional investigators, evidence analysts, and training strengthen the country’s ability to find abused children, rescue them, and pursue their attackers. This is a direct gain in the state’s ability to protect people.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The earmark funds additional child-exploitation positions. Net staffing could also depend on whether existing child-exploitation staff paid from other funds move elsewhere. The reviewed record does not show that S.2 would cause such offsets. The evidence question therefore covers net child-exploitation staffing, assignments and durability, not only whether earmarked new hires stay on the work. Sources: [1].

points.title: It strengthens efforts to take criminal networks’ money.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It strengthens efforts to take criminal networks’ money.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents and operations: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI investigates money laundering, which hides criminal earnings. Its financial investigators “identify and seize illicit proceeds” [18].
  • Because These investigations have taken money away from criminals. In 2024, HSI reported that its El Dorado financial task forces had achieved, over a decade, “over 2,100 arrests and the seizure of more than $2.68 billion in illicit proceeds.” [20]
  • So Supporting investigations that seize criminal earnings removes resources used to keep criminal networks operating. That strengthens the state against organized threats to public safety.
points.con_html:
Response The decade of seizures does not establish an added S.2 effect on the financial investigations that produced them.

  • Because The total comes from work done over a decade: “Over the last decade, EDTF investigations have resulted in over 2,100 arrests and the seizure of more than $2.68 billion in illicit proceeds.” [20] EDTF means El Dorado financial task forces.
  • Because Cato's September 2025 account described ICE taking agents “away from their investigations and enforcement responsibilities to conduct civil immigration enforcement operations” [23], including HSI agents.
  • Because Section 102 funds HSI staff and operations; it sets aside no money or added staff for El Dorado investigations. Its stated spending purposes include “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • So The historical total does not show how S.2 would change financial casework under those assignments. The PRO has not connected the added funding to added seizures.
