The assignment evidence gives a reason to question whether added capacity reaches the named work; it does not show that it cannot, or that Section 102 hires would be reassigned.

points.title: It strengthens defenses against financial scams.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 It strengthens defenses against financial scams.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI’s ongoing investigative work through money “for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1].
  • Because This includes fraud cases that produce convictions and seizures: “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases that resulted in 137 criminal arrests, 121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” [18]
  • So Supporting investigators who pursue scammers and seize their funds strengthens protection against financial predators. That serves [NAME]’s concern for a state able to defend people and the country’s financial security.
points.con_html:
Response The elder-fraud figures do not establish that S.2 would increase the investigators available for scams.

  • Because The figures describe fiscal year 2024: “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases that resulted in 137 criminal arrests, 121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” [18]
  • Because The later staffing account identified HSI among the agencies supplying immigration operations and reported: “This diversion has significantly curtailed the government’s capacity to address criminal activity in the United States.” [23]
  • So A past caseload does not show how the new budget would affect fraud assignments. The PRO supplies no link from its funding provision to an expanded fraud team under the changed priorities.

points.title: It helps defend essential public services from cyberattacks.
points.pro_html:
Point 11 It helps defend essential public services from cyberattacks.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI investigators, support staff, and operations: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI’s Operation Cyber Centurion (OCC) fights hacking and attacks that lock computers for ransom. Its targets include attacks on “major utilities, healthcare, public education, financial systems, emergency services and local government operations.” [18]
  • Because This program has stopped attacks: “In FY 2024, OCC disrupted 195 intrusions and attacks.” [18]
  • So Supporting this work strengthens defenses for services people depend on for power, medical care, emergency help, and government. Keeping those services secure supports the national stability [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The cyberattack disruptions do not establish that S.2 would expand the cyber work that produced them.

  • Because Cato's September 2025 account reported HSI suspending work on “human trafficking, child exploitation, cybercrime” [23] to focus on immigration arrests.
  • Because Section 102 pays general HSI expenses, including “mission support and operations and maintenance” [1], without directing an expansion of Operation Cyber Centurion.
  • So The program's 2024 record does not show that S.2 would restore or expand investigators assigned to cyber cases. Keeping essential services secure requires that missing operational link.

points.title: It strengthens investigations of unsafe equipment sold to the military and police.
points.pro_html:
Point 12 It strengthens investigations of unsafe equipment sold to the military and police.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI agents and criminal investigations outside its immigration and customs enforcement missions: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI and partner agencies investigated a supplier that sold unsafe helmets and body armor to government agencies. The official account states: “This case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, and the General Services Administration Office of Inspector General” [24]. The supplier pleaded guilty to wire fraud: “Meining was charged by criminal information with wire fraud, and, on March 23, 2023, he pleaded guilty to the single charge.” [24]
  • Because A Defense Department investigator described the harm: the supplier’s actions “put U.S. servicemembers at risk, degraded American warfighter readiness, and undermined the missions of our military services.” [24]
  • So More means to investigate this fraud help protect the people and equipment the country relies on for defense. That directly serves [NAME]’s concern for a strong state able to defend its citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The wire-fraud charge does not establish that the equipment investigation qualifies for funds excluding work related to customs enforcement.

  • Because CBP officers “intercepted and detained a package from China addressed to Meining” [24]. To obtain its release, “Meining submitted doctored test results” [24]. The case included false claims about imported goods.
  • Because Section 102 restricts its money to “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]
  • So The offense charged does not settle whether the investigative function was related to customs enforcement. The PRO does not establish that its cited funding reaches this example of protecting military equipment.

points.title: It supports protection at major public events.
points.pro_html:
Point 13 It supports protection at major public events.

  • Because Section 102 funds HSI staff and operations: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI supplies personnel to help the U.S. Secret Service with “National Special Security Events (NSSEs) and protective detail assignments.” [20] Its 2024 report lists support for both parties’ national conventions and the NATO summit in Washington: “the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in Washington, D.C.; the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee, Wisconsin; the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Illinois” [18].
  • So Supporting this pool of trained officers strengthens protection at public gatherings and major government events. That serves [NAME]’s concern for public safety and stable national institutions.
points.con_html:
Response The event details do not establish that S.2 would add officers available for event protection.

  • Because The testimony describes an existing practice: “HSI frequently provides personnel to augment USSS-led National Special Security Events (NSSEs) and protective detail assignments.” [20] USSS is the U.S. Secret Service.
  • Because Section 102 funds HSI's general staff and operations: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1]. It directs no increase in officers assigned to those details.
  • Because A January 2026 Senate letter reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement.
  • So Past event support does not show that the bill would enlarge the available protective force under the changed assignments.

  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement. This is the same assignment evidence cited in the point-specific responses; it is not a finding about the future assignments of Section 102 hires.

points.title: It strengthens emergency response and rescue capacity.
points.pro_html:
Point 14 It strengthens emergency response and rescue capacity.

  • Because It funds “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” [1]
  • Because CBP describes aircraft that support emergency workers through “the rapid-response deployment of equipment, canines, and personnel.” [10] It also describes helicopter capabilities that include “essential aerial relocation, transport, tactical response, rescue, and investigative surveillance functions” [10].
  • So Funding additional air and sea response capacity gives the government more means to bring help and rescue people in danger. That strengthens the country’s ability to protect people during emergencies.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: GAO (2024) reports a global pilot shortage and uncompetitive salaries, with direct-hire authority having helped. The 2025 law funds the same platform purpose. Sources: [7], [6].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 adds about $69.5 billion for border and immigration agencies: “The $69.5 billion in funding would be appropriated in fiscal year (FY) 2026 but be available for use through the end of FY 2029.” [25] Section 202 gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “$31,075,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1], “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]. The added money sustains an existing campaign: “The money will allow the department to continue the Trump administration’s mass deportation strategy” [26].

points.title: It funds more street operations with a record of harming the people the state should protect.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It funds more street operations with a record of harming the people the state should protect.

  • Because Human Rights Watch documented immigration agents “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin, and using excessive force.” [27]
  • Because The harm reaches citizens: the funding dispute followed “the killing of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.” [26]
  • Because S.2 adds funding “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [27]
  • Because It also supplies money outside the yearly funding cycle: the package “provides funding for federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.” [25]
  • So More operating money through 2029 gives these operations more resources and less need to seek yearly approval. That weakens a practical way for Congress to demand safer conduct. Funding further exposure to documented violence undermines the citizen protection [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not linked the added money to further use of the street tactics behind its examples.

  • Because Reported practices had changed in some places before the vote. May reporting from Chicago found: “Community leaders and rapid responders say they are seeing more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall.” [28]
  • Because The Minneapolis operation’s commander had also left: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [29]
  • So The PRO projects earlier tactics onto the added funds without accounting for the reported changes. This response does not answer its funding-cycle argument.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Funding-cycle baseline: CRS says the 2025 detention and enforcement money is available FY2025–FY2029. Sources: [5].

Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It sustains dangerous detention and blocks some uses of an arrest fund that could reduce confinement.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It sustains dangerous detention and blocks some uses of an arrest fund that could reduce confinement.

  • Because S.2 pays for “facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because For its special arrest fund in areas that do not meet the bill's cooperation rules, it bars release spending unless existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” [1].
  • Because Human Rights Watch documented detention conditions including “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” [27].
  • So Paying to sustain confinement under these conditions, while restricting this fund's use for release, exposes people to threats to life and health inside a system the United States controls. Safe federal custody is part of a reliable state; financing unsafe custody undermines that public protection.
points.con_html:
Response The special arrest fund’s spending limit does not establish less access to release.

  • Because The release restriction covers “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” [1] and preserves releases “required by existing law” [1]. It limits the new arrest fund’s spending, without withdrawing other release funds or changing release rights.
  • So The spending limit does not show that releases allowed and funded under existing law become less available. This response does not answer the PRO's separate link between facility funding and sustained unsafe custody.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Detention baseline: a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention costs in FY2027 with 2025-law funds. Sources: [30].

Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It expands local policing that damages crime control.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It expands local policing that damages crime control.

  • Because S.2 funds local immigration-enforcement agreements: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act” [1].
  • Because The street-policing version was already authorized before the vote. A February 2025 ICE agreement lets local officers “interrogate any alien or person believed to be an alien as to his right to be or remain in the United States” [31].
  • Because A study of 2005–2014 crime-victim surveys found that these street task forces raised Latinos' risk of being attacked: “287(g) task force programs significantly increased violent victimization among Latinos” [32].
  • Because Research on Secure Communities, another program linking local police to deportation, found that “Secure Communities reduced the likelihood that Hispanic victims reported crime to the police.” [33]
  • Because Reporting helps police catch offenders: “When crime reporting declines, police are less able to identify, prevent, and solve crimes when they occur, making it harder to apprehend offenders.” [33]
  • So S.2 expands agreements that include a form of policing with documented costs to public safety. The reporting evidence also shows how linking police to deportation can weaken crime control. [NAME] has a reason to oppose weakening the state's ability to protect communities from offenders.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The victimization study measured program starts and flags enforcement intensity as a further question. The reporting study covers Secure Communities' fingerprint sharing. The 2025 law already supported 287(g), and the street model predates S.2. Sources: [32], [33], [5], [31].

Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It expands an enforcement climate that violent impersonators exploit.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It expands an enforcement climate that violent impersonators exploit.

  • Because S.2 adds no ban on masks: “This bill, just like the last one, does not prohibit any agent from wearing a mask.” [34]
  • Because An FBI bulletin reported actual attacks: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” [35].
  • Because The FBI advisory linked rising impersonation crimes to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [35]. WIRED reports confusion “making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.” [35]
  • So Funding more operations without addressing this confusion sustains opportunities for criminals to borrow federal authority. That threatens residents' safety and their ability to recognize genuine protection.
points.con_html:
Response The mask and identification steps mark no change under S.2, and the public-profile part of the FBI's link rests on 2025 conditions.

  • Because The FBI account ties impersonation to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [35] and ICE’s “heightened profile” [35], citing “five 2025 incidents” [35]. It documents crimes under the existing enforcement campaign, rather than a change in identification caused by S.2.
  • Because The report distinguishes existing rules from its advice. Officers must identify themselves “as soon as it is practical and safe to do so.” [35] The FBI also recommends that officers “cooperate with individuals who request further verification” [35]. The bill does not change the identification rule.
  • Because May 2026 reports describe less public operations. Chicago-area community leaders reported “more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall” [28], and Tom Homan attributed “fewer viral videos of ICE agents making arrests” [29] to targeted operations. Neither report says that enforcement stopped.
  • So An absent mask ban does not establish added confusion compared with existing law, and a 2025 public profile may not carry over in full to less visible operations. This narrows the PRO to its enforcement-volume link. It does not show that added operations would create no further opening for impersonators.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It supports assignments that pull investigators away from other serious threats.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It supports assignments that pull investigators away from other serious threats.

  • Because Section 202 pays ICE staff, “including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Section 203 also permits funding “for DHS and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement” [2]. DHS means the Department of Homeland Security.
  • Because The campaign has already diverted federal investigators: “The Trump administration has already diverted thousands of law enforcement officials at multiple agencies away from their work tackling serious crime and national security investigations to focus on immigration” [36].
  • Because These assignments have concrete costs for child-abuse investigations: “These delays can mean the difference between building a case against a predator and letting the trail go cold.” [37]
  • Note Section 102's separate investigation fund is restricted to “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1] That restriction governs that fund; sections 202 and 203 still pay for the immigration assignments above.
  • So S.2 finances a campaign that uses investigators for deportation work at the expense of other protective duties. Sustaining that diversion leaves serious crimes and national security threats less fully covered, contrary to [NAME]'s concern that the country defend itself against all threats.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that S.2 worsens the staffing shortage behind the reported diversion of investigators.

  • Because Section 202 funds “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping” [1] immigration personnel. More funded immigration work can therefore draw on new staff; it is not evidence of additional transfers from other cases.
  • Because Section 102 adds $7.45 billion for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI): “$7,450,000,000” [1]. Its money “shall be used for functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]
  • Because Within that sum, “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” [1]. This funds additional people for the work the PRO says lacks staff.
  • So The protected investigation fund matters to the claimed staffing loss even though other funds can pay for immigration assignments. The PRO has not shown that the new hiring money leaves a larger staffing gap or causes more investigators to abandon other protective work.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It funds tools used to intimidate peaceful scrutiny of government.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It funds tools used to intimidate peaceful scrutiny of government.

  • Because The added money supports broader monitoring: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [26]
  • Because Threats against observers are documented: “a government lawyer told a federal judge in Maine that agents had violated Department of Homeland Security policy by threatening to put the observers' information into a database.” [38]
  • Because Such threats discourage scrutiny. A lawyer seeking disclosure of ICE's surveillance practices explained: “If people think that protesting or filming law enforcement may put them in a secret database, many will stay silent” [38].
  • So Funding further monitoring equips officials to intimidate people who document their conduct. A state that silences peaceful warnings about its own abuses becomes less answerable for protecting citizens. That threatens safe, stable government.
points.con_html:
Response The observer example does not establish that S.2 expands the monitoring used to discourage scrutiny.

  • Because The quoted lawyer says threats can deter observers “regardless of whether such databases even exist.” [38] The report establishes a threat, without establishing the database or technology behind it.
  • Because S.2 funds IT maintenance for “enforcement and removal operations” [1]. Its additional DHS appropriation is also tied to listed uses: “for the purposes provided in this title or in paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21.” [1] These spending permissions do not identify an added project to track peaceful observers.
  • So The PRO has not connected an increase in monitoring capacity funded by S.2 to further intimidation or less effective scrutiny. A threat that can work without the claimed database does not supply that link.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It disrupts the everyday work and institutions that keep communities stable.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It disrupts the everyday work and institutions that keep communities stable.

  • Because During the Minneapolis enforcement operation, “Workers stayed home. Small businesses shuttered, and tens of thousands of residents were suddenly thrown into food and housing insecurity.” [34]
  • Because KFF reports that immigrants and family members avoided activities including “going to church or other community activities, going to work, or taking their child to school or school events due to immigration-related fears.” [39]
  • So Fear that keeps people from work, school, and community life makes towns less able to function. Funding further operations with this pattern threatens the social stability [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's Minneapolis evidence may not carry over to added operations, and its survey predates the reported change in tactics.

  • Because Before the vote, the president had ordered the Minneapolis operation wound down: “Earlier this year, Mr. Trump charged Homan with winding down the Minneapolis operation” [29]. Independent May reporting also found that Border Patrol groups in Chicago “no longer are making surprise visits to Michigan Avenue or marching through Little Village, Back of the Yards and other neighborhoods.” [28]
  • Because KFF’s activity-avoidance evidence came from the “KFF/New York Times 2025 Survey of Immigrants (August 28-October 20, 2025).” [39] It measured fears before the changes above.
  • So Continued immigration enforcement does not establish continued use of the particular surge tactics, so the Minneapolis disruption is weak evidence about added operations. This does not show that fear has receded, and the survey still supports a link between enforcement fears and avoided activities.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: Removing workers weakens essential services and the economic resources behind national strength.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Removing workers weakens essential services and the economic resources behind national strength.

  • Because S.2 funds removals: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because The existing campaign has already detained an essential worker: “He is a medical laboratory scientist who worked on the front lines during the COVID-19 pandemic” [36]; “Yet he remains detained, as of April 2026.” [36]
  • Because Immigrants work in basic industries: “Immigrants, both documented and undocumented, contribute to the U.S. economy by working jobs in construction, hospitality, landscaping, and farming” [40]. Research on earlier enforcement found “a slowdown in new housing construction” [40].
  • Because The damage extends to national resources: “Crackdowns on immigration are harmful to U.S. workers and contractionary for the overall U.S. economy as the labor market weakens and slower population growth drags down demand and public finances.” [40]
  • So Financing wider removals threatens workers who supply care, food, and shelter. The resulting loss of production and tax resources also weakens the country's means to fund protection and withstand shocks. Both bear directly on the strong, secure country [NAME] values.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The GDP figure is a 1.3 million deportation scenario, not an S.2 estimate. The medical worker's detention predates the bill. Transport has a planned $350 million FY2027 offset. Sources: [40], [36], [30].

Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: Enforcement fears weaken defenses against disease.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Enforcement fears weaken defenses against disease.

  • Because KFF found that “14% of immigrant adults overall say they or a family member have avoided seeking medical care since January 2025 due to immigration-related concerns.” [39]
  • Because Dallas County's public-health director “ties the dramatic drop in county-administered vaccinations to concerns about immigration enforcement.” [41]
  • Because He warned that communities are “more vulnerable to outbreaks” [41] when people avoid care.
  • Because In a February–March 2026 probability survey of Minneapolis and St. Paul adults about a federal enforcement surge, 30.6% of Minneapolis respondents with a regularly scheduled vaccination and 21.1% in St. Paul reported missing it over enforcement concerns. This measures self-reported avoidance, not population vaccination coverage. [42]
  • So Sustaining enforcement that drives people away from clinics weakens disease prevention. Protection against infectious disease is part of protecting the country against threats, giving [NAME] another reason to oppose this funding.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Dallas figures are county-clinic counts (16,412 in 2024; 9,578 in the most recent August) with the enforcement link attributed to the director. The Twin Cities figures are self-reports among those with a regularly scheduled vaccination and are not population coverage. No all-provider registry series was found (Q30). The brief's New point on the funded baseline still applies to this point. Sources: [42], [39], [41].

Brief context note: the 2025 law provided ICE $45 billion and $29.85 billion, and a June 9 analysis reports plans to offset $416 million in detention and $350 million in transport in FY2027 with it. Size unresolved. Sources: [5], [30].

points.title: It supports a detention plan that threatens local water and sewage systems.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 It supports a detention plan that threatens local water and sewage systems.

  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]
  • Because ICE's planned network includes a large facility in Social Circle, Georgia. The city's February assessment states that “the total additional water demand required for a facility of this scale simply exceeds what the City’s system is capable of providing.” [43]
  • Because Its May 2026 lawsuit warns of “sewer main backups” [44] and “contamination of groundwater and local waterways.” [44]
  • So Money for running the planned detention network supports demands that essential local systems cannot meet. Threats to drinking water and sewage disposal undermine public health and the basic services on which stable communities depend.
points.con_html:
Response The Social Circle evidence does not show that S.2 increases the utility risk from that already funded project.

  • Because The city’s May 13 complaint identifies the warehouse initiative’s funding: the efforts “rely on $45 billion appropriated by Congress in July 2025” [44]. The plan and its utility problems therefore existed under an earlier appropriation.
  • Because In March, the city blocked the water connection and explained: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity” [45]. The infrastructure obstacle existed before S.2.
  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1] It does not change the project’s water access or review requirements.
  • So The warnings concern a particular project’s design and operation. The PRO has not shown that S.2 changes whether it opens, how many people it holds, or how it gets water and disposes of waste. The earlier project’s risk cannot simply be counted as a risk added by this bill.

points.title: Its added debt increases pressure on financial stability and readiness for emergencies.
points.pro_html:
Point 11 Its added debt increases pressure on financial stability and readiness for emergencies.

  • Because The American Action Forum estimates the bill's borrowing cost: “After accounting for roughly $25 billion of additional interest costs, the package would increase budget deficits by $94.5 billion over the FY 2026–2035 budget window.” [25]
  • Because The Congressional Budget Office explains the general risk: “Larger amounts of debt make the United States’ fiscal position more vulnerable to an increase in interest rates.” [46]
  • Because It also warns that “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.” [46]
  • So S.2 adds borrowing and interest costs to the financial pressures facing future defense and emergency decisions. Increasing that burden weakens the financial resilience needed for a state that can protect its citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO moves from fiscal cost and sensitivity to interest rates to weaker national readiness without establishing that last step.

  • Because The estimate puts borrowing and interest costs at “$94.5 billion over the FY 2026–2035 budget window.” [25] That measures added expense over ten years, rather than a loss of protective funding or borrowing options.
  • Because The Congressional Budget Office describes greater sensitivity to interest rates: “Larger amounts of debt make the United States’ fiscal position more vulnerable to an increase in interest rates.” [46] Its readiness warning depends on future decisions: “The size of the debt might make lawmakers feel constrained from using deficit-financed fiscal policy to respond to unforeseen events, promote economic activity, or further other goals.” [46]
  • Because Its final S.2 estimate states: “CBO has not reviewed S. 2 for effects on spending subject to appropriation.” [47] That estimate does not assess whether later defense or emergency funding would fall.
  • So The PRO has not shown how the bill’s added costs translate into less room to finance protection, through borrowing limits or changed spending decisions. A budget cost and a general warning about rising national debt do not establish that further effect on readiness.

pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: S.2 provides about $70 billion through 2029 for immigration enforcement and border security. It increases the number of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers; expands resources for detention and deportation operations; invests in border security technology; and supports other federal immigration enforcement activities.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect S.2 adds funds through September 2029 to what the law in force on June 9, 2026, already provided: “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]. The Congressional Research Service describes their uses: “This bill provides funding to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through FY2029 for immigration enforcement, border security, and related activities.” [2]

points.title: It backs the respect for public authority taught in [NAME]’s religious tradition.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It backs the respect for public authority taught in [NAME]’s religious tradition.

  • Because Sections 201 and 202 fund officers, training, and operations “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Christian writer Daniel Darling traces respect for law to Scripture: “Writing in the first century to the church, Peter instructs Christians to uphold the rule of law.” [3]
  • Because He applies that duty to government: “Governments have the right and duty to uphold the rule of law.” [3]
  • So Funding officials to apply immigration law gives practical support to the public authority that this inherited teaching calls on Christians to respect.
points.con_html:
Response The duty to respect lawful authority does not supply the PRO’s missing link between a larger enforcement budget and maintaining that religious practice.

  • Because Christian writer Daniel Darling quotes the instruction: “Submit to every human authority because of the Lord” [3].
  • Because He also distinguishes the duties of citizens and government: “It’s important for us to understand the difference between the obligations of the state and the obligations of individual Christians.” [3]
  • Because Section 201 pays for personnel and operations “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • So Obeying lawful authority, government enforcing laws, and increasing an agency’s budget are different steps. The PRO supplies no rule connecting the budget increase to greater adherence to the inherited duty of respect.
points.retirement_reason: Religious endorsement of authority, borders or protection from crime does not establish preservation, observance or transmission of a particular inherited practice.

points.title: It helps guard national borders, as this Christian tradition teaches government should.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps guard national borders, as this Christian tradition teaches government should.

  • Because Section 103 funds “Upgrades and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1]
  • Because Darling explains the religious basis for national boundaries: “In Acts 17:26, Paul says that it is God who puts people in their nations and boundaries, implying the legitimacy of borders.” [3]
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention calls for resources to carry out border protection: “we encourage elected officials to prioritize measures that secure our borders and to provide adequate resources to border patrol and those working in our immigration system” [4].
  • So Giving officers tools to guard those boundaries puts a public duty recognized by [NAME]’s religious tradition into practice.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The 2023 resolution asks for 'adequate' resources and predates the 2025 law's $6.17 billion for border security, technology and screening. Whether adequacy was met is unaddressed. Sources: [4], [5].
points.retirement_reason: Religious endorsement of authority, borders or protection from crime does not establish preservation, observance or transmission of a particular inherited practice.

points.title: It funds custody of convicted abusers, supporting the protective role this tradition assigns to government.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It funds custody of convicted abusers, supporting the protective role this tradition assigns to government.

  • Because Section 202(9) sets aside money for ICE to make “arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” [1]. These are areas that do not meet the bill’s cooperation rules.
  • Because The covered group includes adults who can be removed for certain crimes: “is deportable under section 237(a)(2) of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(2));” [1].
  • Because Those grounds include convictions for domestic violence and child abuse: “Any alien who at any time after admission is convicted of a crime of domestic violence, a crime of stalking, or a crime of child abuse, child neglect, or child abandonment is deportable.” [6]
  • Because The Family Research Council states the religious duty: “The Bible teaches that the government has a duty to protect its people from those who would attack and harm them.” [7]
  • So Strengthening ICE’s ability to take convicted abusers in that group into custody backs the protective duty [NAME]’s inherited faith assigns to government.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.retirement_reason: Religious endorsement of authority, borders or protection from crime does not establish preservation, observance or transmission of a particular inherited practice.

points.title: It supports inherited Christian sexual standards by funding work against child sexual exploitation.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It supports inherited Christian sexual standards by funding work against child sexual exploitation.

  • Because Section 102 sets aside $108.5 million for additional child exploitation investigators and experts who examine evidence “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1].
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention teaches that “God calls His people to holiness and Christ has specifically summoned His followers to sexual purity” [8].
  • Because It calls on government to “enact and enforce laws that restrict all forms of pornography, particularly those that include and exploit minors” [8].
  • So Paying investigators to combat child sexual exploitation puts resources behind a sexual standard [NAME]’s religious tradition calls on government to uphold.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.retirement_reason: The substantive benefit is protection of children from sexual exploitation. A religious sexual-purity quotation does not establish how this investigative funding affects continuing a particular custom or observance.

points.title: It supports the Christian duty to oppose slavery by equipping investigators who fight forced labor.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It supports the Christian duty to oppose slavery by equipping investigators who fight forced labor.

  • Because Section 102 adds money to “hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1]. It limits that money to “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]
  • Because Homeland Security Investigations conducts “criminal investigations related to sex trafficking and forced labor” [9].
  • Because This work addresses exploitation that can occur within the country: “Human trafficking is exploitation-based, with or without a border crossing” [10].
  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention grounds its opposition to trafficking in the Bible’s affirmation of “the sanctity and dignity of all human life” [11] and its call on believers to “speak up for those who cannot defend themselves” [11].
  • Because It urges support for “public policies at the local, state, national, and international level which combat human trafficking” [11].
  • So Supporting investigators’ work against forced labor puts this inherited religious duty to defend people from slavery into practice.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: ICE testimony says labor-trafficking cases are fewer because of detection difficulty. The DHS total combines sex and labor trafficking. The reviewed record does not identify the share of §102 funds allocated to forced-labor work. Sources: [10], [9].
points.retirement_reason: Protection from forced labor is the substantive benefit; a Christian anti-slavery duty adds no distinct Tradition connection.

points.title: It funds drug detection that could help preserve family transmission of faith.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It funds drug detection that could help preserve family transmission of faith.

  • Because Section 103 funds inspection equipment to combat “the entry or exit of illicit narcotics” [1] and border work for “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1].
  • Because The Government Accountability Office explains how the equipment works: “These scans produce images that CBP officers review to help detect illegal drugs or other contraband.” [12]
  • Because It also identifies a threat to family life: “Opioid abuse destroys the individual user, but it also destroys the family unit by often separating children from their addicted parents” [13].
  • Because Its statement on the family gives parents the task of passing on faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.” [14]
  • So By addressing opioid abuse that separates children from parents, drug-detection work could help preserve the family setting for parents’ continuing religious teaching. That transmission, rather than a general religious endorsement of drug control, supplies the Tradition connection.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish its chain from more drug detection to less opioid abuse and preserved family teaching.

  • Because Finding drugs does not establish a lasting loss of supply. Drug-policy researcher Jonathan Caulkins explains the problem: “There is little point in working hard to seize drugs that can be replaced at a very low cost.” [15]
  • Because The Government Accountability Office also finds that the Department of Homeland Security’s “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.” [16]
  • Because The family practice at the end of the PRO’s chain is teaching faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [14].
  • So The PRO needs evidence that the added detection reduces abuse despite cheap replacement of seized drugs. A scanner’s ability to reveal contraband does not establish that step. Without it, the PRO has not connected this spending to preserving the family practice of passing on faith.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, S.2 adds resources for the existing immigration arrest, detention and deportation system. Section 202 gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “$31,075,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1], including “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” [1] and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations” [1]. ICE’s enforcement work includes “the identification, arrest, detention, and removal of noncitizens” [17]. Section 201 gives Customs and Border Protection “$13,020,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029” [1] “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities” [1]. Both grants are “In addition to amounts otherwise available” [1]. This gives the operations described below added financial support and room to grow.

points.title: Added removals threaten family unity and parents’ passing on the faith.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Added removals threaten family unity and parents’ passing on the faith.

  • Because A joint evangelical and Catholic report identifies the risk of “marriages being divided or children being raised apart from one or both parents due to deportations” [18].
  • Because Southern Baptists affirm that “God has ordained the family as the foundational institution of human society” [19].
  • Because Their Baptist Faith and Message, adopted in 2000, ties passing on faith to parents’ daily example: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.” [20]
  • So More resources for removals put Christian families at greater risk of being forced apart.
  • So Living apart disrupts shared family life and parents’ daily teaching. Preserving these family duties gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the added funding.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: ICE's director said the 2025 law provided $15.4 billion for removals. §202 does not separate continued from added removals. The reviewed record does not identify an estimate of added removals specific to Christian families. Sources: [21].

Brief context note: ICE's director described about 11,000 new hires under the 2025 law, Senate Budget minority staff report $62 billion of it unobligated at the end of May 2026, and the administration calls S.2 funding for 'base operations'. Size unresolved. Sources: [21], [22], [23].

points.title: Added enforcement threatens shared worship, religious teaching and familiar church rites.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Added enforcement threatens shared worship, religious teaching and familiar church rites.

  • Because Southern Baptist leaders reported that fear of enforcement left even lawful immigrants “afraid to gather to worship God and receive spiritual care in their local church” [24].
  • Because A June 8, 2026 report quotes an amended church lawsuit describing a change in religious practice: “Baptisms that previously would have been occasions for communal worship and celebration are now being held in private.” [25]
  • Because Southern Baptists’ confession says Sunday “should include exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.” [20]
  • Because Their religious liberty commission warned that church enforcement would inhibit teaching and evangelism: “our central mission of Gospel proclamation and biblical formation will be inhibited.” [26]
  • Note The February church injunction covered identified plaintiff properties, defined as places “regularly used by Plaintiffs to conduct religious services” [27]. It did not protect every church. The June 8 report describes continued fear and disrupted worship despite that order.
  • So Adding resources to enforcement that already keeps people from church puts shared worship, teaching and rites under greater pressure. [NAME] has a reason to oppose that threat to practicing and passing on the faith.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: ICE's director described about 11,000 new hires under the 2025 law, Senate Budget minority staff report $62 billion of it unobligated at the end of May 2026, and the administration calls S.2 funding for 'base operations'. Size unresolved. Sources: [21], [22], [23].

points.title: Removing pastors and members threatens the continuity of congregations.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Removing pastors and members threatens the continuity of congregations.

  • Because The risk reaches evangelical church leaders. The Associated Press reported that a bishop had told churches with pastors at risk of deportation “to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.” [28]
  • Because The joint Christian report explains the further risk: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.” [18]
  • Because This loss reaches members who remain: “even church members who are citizens or legal permanent residents will be deeply impacted.” [18]
  • So Added removal capacity puts congregations’ leaders and membership at greater risk. Losing a congregation breaks the continuity of a community that carries Christian teaching, worship and customs. Preserving that community gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
points.con_html:
Response The sources do not establish that S.2 would cause the loss of leadership or membership needed for their church-closure warning.

  • Because The bishop’s instruction was a plan to preserve leadership: “The bishop has instructed each congregation with endangered pastors to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.” [28]
  • Because The report makes closure depend on further conditions: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.” [18] It labels this discussion “beyond the scope of this report” [18].
  • So Neither the succession plan nor the conditional warning establishes that S.2 would leave congregations without leaders or enough members to survive. The missing step is a threat to the congregation’s survival from these added funds.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: ICE's director described about 11,000 new hires under the 2025 law, Senate Budget minority staff report $62 billion of it unobligated at the end of May 2026, and the administration calls S.2 funding for 'base operations'. Size unresolved. Sources: [21], [22], [23].

points.title: Added enforcement can interrupt an established church food-distribution ministry.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Added enforcement can interrupt an established church food-distribution ministry.

  • Because Church leaders said a January 2026 Border Patrol arrest on church grounds stopped their aid work. KTLA reported: “The raid interrupted the church’s food distribution ministry and an event for mothers and children in the church garden.” [29]
  • Because The 2018 Southern Baptist immigration resolution teaches that “Scripture is clear on the believer’s hospitality towards immigrants” [19] and urges pastors “to exhort their congregations to serve their local immigrant communities” [19].
  • So More resources for operations that have interrupted this church’s ministry increase the risk of further interruptions to its continuing communal religious work. Maintaining that established ministry, rather than endorsing care for strangers in the abstract, supplies [NAME]’s Tradition reason.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.
points.notes_html: Brief context note: ICE's director described about 11,000 new hires under the 2025 law, Senate Budget minority staff report $62 billion of it unobligated at the end of May 2026, and the administration calls S.2 funding for 'base operations'. Size unresolved. Sources: [21], [22], [23].

points.title: Added custody puts pastoral care and the Christian duty to visit prisoners at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Added custody puts pastoral care and the Christian duty to visit prisoners at risk.

  • Because Access barriers reached both Protestant and Catholic ministry. Christianity Today reported that Indonesian pastors waited in vain to visit a detained member; a Pentecostal pastor also failed to enter: “Like the Indonesian pastors, the pastor he met never got in.” [30]
  • Because The problem continued into 2026. An April court order found that Broadview’s blanket ban “renders plaintiffs’ religious exercise of providing ministry to detainees and migrants effectively impracticable.” [31]
  • Because An April 2026 release from Rep. Jimmy Gomez's office says clergy were denied entry to Los Angeles's Roybal facility on Ash Wednesday and that four were admitted on Good Friday after the office pressed ICE. This shows both an access barrier and a remedy that took congressional intervention, rather than a permanent ban at that site. [32]
  • Because DHS defended excluding religious services from field offices: “It is not within standard operating procedure for religious services to be provided in a field office” [33]. The same report describes evidence that people were held in those facilities “for days on end” [33].
  • Note Court relief named particular facilities. The April 7 order required access to “the Broadview facility” [31]; the March 20 order required a clergy-access process for “the Whipple facility” [34]. Those orders did not open every place where added arrests could send Christians.
  • Because Southern Baptist leaders grounded their appeal in Jesus’ words: “I was in prison and you came to visit me” [24].
  • So Supporting more custody exposes more Christians and their pastors to these access barriers. [NAME] has a reason to oppose that risk to prayer, pastoral care and an inherited duty of the church.
points.con_html:
Response Documented access remedies limit the forecast from earlier bans, while leaving access elsewhere uncertain.

  • Because Broadview’s interim agreement produced visits before the vote: “Faith leaders began daily visits Friday, May 15, 2026” [35]. It allowed spiritual care once a day, including “bringing the Sacraments and other religious items approved beforehand.” [35]
  • Because Whipple’s April 16 order stated: “Access is the default.” [36] It required same-day access or a specific, time-limited reason for delay.
  • Because According to the congressional office involved, Roybal supplies a third-site example of both denial and relief: clergy admitted for Good Friday followed an Ash Wednesday denial and the office's intervention. One reported visit does not establish routine access at Roybal. [32]
  • So Added custody cannot simply be assigned the former bans at sites where access improved. The response is partial: it does not answer added custody at sites without such measures or where access depends on case-by-case intervention. Neither the reported barriers nor these remedies show a uniform nationwide pattern.

points.title: Added detention support puts life and human dignity at risk, including unborn life.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Added detention support puts life and human dignity at risk, including unborn life.

  • Because Human Rights Watch documented “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” [37] in immigration detention in 2025. Its assessment of S.2 warned: “This risks allowing patterns of violence, medical neglect, inhumane detention, and impunity to continue.” [37]
  • Because February 2026 reporting described documented “miscarriages, denial of prenatal care, and inadequate food and medical attention” [38] among detained pregnant women.
  • Because Southern Baptists’ 2000 confession states: “We should speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death.” [20]
  • Because It also teaches that “every person of every race possesses full dignity and is worthy of respect and Christian love.” [20]
  • So Financing more custody in a system with these documented harms increases exposure to neglect and degrading treatment. Protecting life and honoring every person’s sacred worth are inherited Christian duties, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose that support.
points.con_html: No point-specific CON is provided.

Evidence note: The 2025 law provided $45 billion for detention capacity. The pregnancy report describes failures to follow existing policy, and HRW's point concerns omitted reforms. Sources: [5], [38], [37].

points.title: Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.

  • Because This danger has already reached Christian converts. In November 2025, the BBC reported a husband’s account: “They deported my wife back to Iran even though she is a Christian” [39]. The BBC reported that she had since “been contacted and summoned by Iranian intelligence.” [39]
  • Because The report explains the religious danger: “Converting from Islam is treated as apostasy, and converts face arrest, interrogation and prison terms.” [39]
  • Because The risk also reaches relatives who accompany a deported family member. The joint Christian report warns that this can mean “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18]
  • Because Southern Baptists’ 2011 religious liberty resolution affirms the freedom “to worship without harassment or impediment from the state” [40] and calls for prayer for Christians “persecuted, imprisoned, or facing execution for their testimony of faith in Jesus.” [40]
  • So Additional removal capacity supports a system that has returned Christians to danger and puts accompanying relatives’ worship at risk. Preserving their freedom to live by their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
points.con_html:
Response The persecution evidence does not connect S.2’s transport funding to added unsafe returns or moves by accompanying relatives.

  • Because The BBC reports that Ali’s wife was returned to Iran and summoned by Iranian intelligence. Her lawyer said sensitive information about religious conversion and other asylum grounds “was not removed before deportation.” [39] This account concerns the handling of protection, destinations and religious information.
  • Because Existing law bars removal to a country when the official finds the specified threat, subject to listed exceptions: “the Attorney General may not remove an alien to a country if the Attorney General decides that the alien's life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien's race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” [41]
  • Because The family report’s accompanying-relative warning depends on the destination: “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18] Section 202’s transport funding does not choose destinations or replace protection decisions.
  • So The PRO has not shown that the funds would expand or sustain those unsafe routes beyond existing removal operations. More removal funding alone does not establish more returns to religious persecution, including for relatives who move with a deported family member.

points.title: Added enforcement resources threaten inherited Christian standards of equal respect and just government.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Added enforcement resources threaten inherited Christian standards of equal respect and just government.

  • Because Human Rights Watch documented immigration agents “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [37] during the 2025 Los Angeles operations.
  • Because Southern Baptists’ longstanding confession says “Christians should oppose racism” [20] and calls on Christians to bring government under “the principles of righteousness, truth, and brotherly love.” [20]
  • Because Their 2026 immigration resolution reaffirms support for enforcement on those terms: “lawful immigration enforcement carried out justly, humanely, and according to due process” [42].
  • So Giving added reach to enforcement with documented race-based arrest practices puts more people at risk of unequal treatment. [NAME]’s commitment to maintaining these Christian moral standards gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that funding.
points.con_html:
Response The Los Angeles evidence does not show that the race-based practice it documents would carry over to the reach S.2 adds.

  • Because Human Rights Watch’s finding concerns the summer 2025 Los Angeles campaign, including “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [37]. That finding does not say whether the practice continued in June 2026.
  • Because CBS reported Tom Homan’s account in May 2026 that “since the Minneapolis operation was scaled back, Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [43] This is an official’s account, and agents still arrest other people they find during operations.
  • So The PRO moves from a 2025 practice to the added funds without showing that the practice persists. This does not show that race-based detention has ended or that added reach carries no such risk. The inherited Christian ban on racism does not fill that gap.
